Vivarta AI: The Number in the Contract

Bengaluru, August 2026. For three years one metric has told Vivarta AI which customers would stay, what to build, and — because of a decision taken in 2023 — what to invoice. It has stopped working, and nobody agrees on what that means.

1. Sunday night

At 11.20 on the night of Sunday, 9 August 2026, Aditi Bhatnagar sat at the dining table of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with a laptop, a printed spreadsheet, and a WhatsApp thread she had muted twice and unmuted twice. On the screen were two charts that could not both be true about the same company.

At 9.30 the next morning she had a one-hour meeting with Ramanathan Iyer, Vivarta AI's founder and chief executive. On Thursday, 13 August, the board would meet by video — three directors in Bengaluru, one in Singapore, one dialling in from Menlo Park — to approve the data room for a Series D round of ₹450 crore that the company expected to sign a term sheet on in October. In that data room sat a slide, used in every investor conversation since 2024, that read: Accounts reaching 55% day-60 auto-resolution renew at 94%.

Ritika Malhotra's memo, delivered from Toronto on Friday evening, said that sentence was no longer true, might never have been true in the way it had been used, and that the number in it had in any case been computed differently since January 2025. Aditi had spent Saturday checking the memo and Sunday discovering that four people in the company had known some part of it for at least six months.

What she did not know was what to do about it — whether this was a measurement problem, a product problem, a pricing problem, or the ordinary sound a company makes when it grows past the thing that made it work.

2. Company history, and the decision that still binds

Vivarta AI was founded in Bengaluru in 2020 by Ram Iyer, previously a support-operations leader at a large Indian IT services firm, and two engineers from Pune. Its product resolved customer-support conversations automatically: it ingested a company's knowledge base, ticket history and order systems, and answered incoming chats, emails and voice calls end-to-end, escalating to a human when it could not.

By March 2026 Vivarta had ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, 143 enterprise accounts and about 620 mid-market accounts, a headcount of 410 — 240 in Bengaluru, 70 in Pune, the rest scattered across Toronto, Berlin, Singapore, Dubai and New Jersey — and reported net revenue retention of 114 per cent. Its customers included Indian NBFCs, D2C brands, two insurance companies, a large logistics firm, and, since 2024, an expanding footprint in the Gulf through Shams Retail Group, a Dubai-based multi-brand retailer with operations in five countries and Vivarta's single largest account at ₹7.4 crore of annual contract value.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken in the second half of 2023. Vivarta was losing enterprise deals to better-known platforms — prospects would not pay a platform fee for software whose value they could not predict. Ram's answer was outcome pricing: Vivarta would charge per auto-resolved conversation, at ₹18 to ₹34 depending on volume, with a small platform fee. It worked. Three of Vivarta's six largest accounts, representing ₹22 crore of ARR, signed on that basis, and the sales team's win rate against incumbents nearly doubled.

It also fused two things that a careful company keeps apart. Auto-resolution rate became simultaneously the product's headline quality metric, the proxy by which Vivarta predicted whether an account would renew, the target its engineering squads were measured on, and the unit on which it raised invoices. Changing the definition of a resolution now meant changing what customers owed.

3. The industry

The Indian market for AI customer-service software in 2026 was crowded and consolidating. Freshworks and Zoho sold broad suites with AI layered in and could bundle aggressively; Yellow.ai and Haptik had strong voice and vernacular capability; global platforms competed at the top of the enterprise segment. Buyers had become far more sophisticated in eighteen months: procurement teams at Indian banks and insurers now ran structured pilots with their own test sets, and several had begun asking for contractual quality floors rather than volume commitments.

Two regulatory facts shaped the product. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the rules that followed constrained what Vivarta could do with customer conversation transcripts: purpose limitation meant transcripts collected to serve a customer's support function could not be freely repurposed to train cross-account models or to build behavioural indices without a fresh consent and contractual basis, and several enterprise contracts went further than the law required. Separately, Vivarta's banking and NBFC customers operated under RBI expectations on outsourcing and IT governance, which meant data residency in India, audit rights, and a documented change-management process for anything that touched customer outcomes — including, Vivarta's compliance counsel had noted in 2025, the definition of a resolution.

The macro picture was ambiguous in a way that mattered. Foundation-model inference costs had fallen roughly 70 per cent in two years, which had raised Vivarta's gross margin from 54 to 71 per cent and, at the same time, made automatic resolution dramatically easier for everyone — including a customer's own in-house team. What had been a differentiated capability in 2023 was becoming a commodity in 2026. Vivarta's own median account had seen day-60 auto-resolution rise from 47 per cent in 2023 to 68 per cent in 2026 with no change in the customer's satisfaction scores.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence, as Aditi reconstructed it over the weekend, ran as follows.

March 2023. Vivarta's first cohort analysis, run by a contractor, found that enterprise accounts whose day-60 auto-resolution exceeded 55 per cent renewed at 94 per cent, against 61 per cent below the threshold. The finding was believed, reasonably, and became the company's organising idea. Roadmaps for 2024 and 2025 were built around raising day-60 resolution: faster knowledge ingestion, intent auto-discovery, aggressive fallback handling.

October 2023. Outcome pricing shipped. The billing definition of a resolution — a conversation closed without human involvement and without a re-contact on the same issue within 72 hours — was written into three enterprise contracts.

January 2025. Tanmay Ghosh's team in Pune rebuilt the resolution pipeline to handle voice and to support a new "assisted" mode, in which the AI drafted and a human approved. In the rebuild, conversations in which a human approved an AI draft without editing it began to be counted as auto-resolutions. Tanmay wrote this in the migration design document, which was reviewed by two engineers. Nobody outside the pipeline team read it. Reported resolution rates rose about four points across the base in the following quarter; the rise was attributed, in the Q4 FY25 board pack, to the intent auto-discovery work shipped in November.

June 2025 onwards. Cheryl Tan's customer-success team in Singapore, whose quarterly targets included the share of accounts above the 55 per cent threshold at day 60, began running what they called "intent sprints": two weeks of manual intent tuning immediately before an account's day-60 read. It worked reliably. It was documented in the team's own playbook and was visible to anyone who looked at the timestamps.

February 2026. Two large accounts — an NBFC in Mumbai and a D2C brand in Gurugram — declined to expand at renewal despite day-60 resolution of 74 and 81 per cent. Both cited the same thing in their exit conversations: the escalations that did reach humans arrived with poor context, and their own agents were re-doing work.

July 2026. Ritika ran the renewal analysis again, on the accounts onboarded in the first half of 2025. The relationship between day-60 resolution and twelve-month renewal had gone flat. On the top decile it appeared, weakly, to invert.

7 August 2026. Ritika's memo landed. It made three claims: that resolution rate had lost its predictive power; that some of the historical relationship had been an artefact of a period when resolution was hard and only well-run implementations achieved it; and that a composite index she had fitted — using escalation quality, re-contact rate, breadth of intents in production, admin configuration activity and eight other signals — predicted twelve-month renewal far better. She noted, in a footnote, that the index could not legally be built from conversation content for eleven accounts whose contracts forbade it.

5. The people

Aditi Bhatnagar, VP Product, Bengaluru. Joined 2022 from a payments company. Owns the roadmap and the metric. Position: the company needs a proxy it can trust before it commits a Series D roadmap to it. Not saying: she approved the 2024 and 2025 roadmaps that optimised the proxy, and a public repudiation is also a repudiation of two years of her own prioritisation.

Ram Iyer, founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Position: the metric has worked, the market is noisy, and the company should not blow up its own story nine weeks before a term sheet. Not saying: he has told two prospective lead investors the 94 per cent figure in the past month, and a restatement in the data room would require him to go back to them.

Shalini Prasad, CFO, Bengaluru. Position: any change to the definition of a resolution is a revenue event before it is a product event. Three contracts, ₹22 crore of ARR, invoice on that definition; if assisted resolutions have been billed as auto-resolutions since January 2025, the exposure is real and must be quantified before anything is said publicly. Not saying: she has already asked external counsel for a view, and has not told Ram.

Tanmay Ghosh, Director of Engineering, Pune. Position: the pipeline change was correct engineering, documented at the time, and the assisted mode is genuinely valuable to customers. Not saying: he raised the counting question in a comment on the design document and, receiving no response in four days, shipped.

Ritika Malhotra, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the company should stop governing on a single behavioural threshold and adopt her composite index for both renewal forecasting and roadmap decisions. Not saying: her training set includes only accounts that survived to twelve months in a form her pipeline could parse, which excludes six accounts that churned in the first two quarters — the very accounts whose behaviour would most test the index.

Lukas Bergmann, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: fourteen customer interviews show that what enterprise buyers value is the quality of the handover when the AI gives up, not the share of conversations it keeps. Wants the roadmap reframed around escalation experience. Not saying: eleven of the fourteen interviews were with European and Gulf buyers, and the two Indian NBFC interviews said something noticeably different about cost per contact.

Cheryl Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: the day-60 threshold is the only number that gives her team leverage with customers' operations heads, and abandoning it would leave her with nothing to run quarterly business reviews on. Not saying: the intent sprints materially inflate day-60 readings, and her team's FY26 bonus was paid on threshold attainment.

Vikram Sethi, Head of Sales, New Jersey. Position: the 55 per cent benchmark is in the sales deck, the ROI calculator and two live proposals worth ₹14 crore; changing the metric mid-quarter is unserious. Not saying: one of those two proposals contains a contractual resolution-rate floor that Vivarta's legal team has not yet reviewed.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"I am not disputing Ritika's arithmetic. I am disputing that eighty-eight accounts at twelve months tells us anything about what the 2023 accounts did at twenty-four. We are comparing a hundred-metre time to a marathon and concluding the runner is slower."

Ram Iyer, in the Friday-evening call, 7 August 2026

"The 2023 relationship may have been real and may also have been a measurement of implementation quality, not of resolution. In 2023 you needed a good implementation to get to 55 per cent. In 2026 you get to 68 per cent by doing nothing, because the models got better. A threshold that everyone clears has no information in it."

Ritika Malhotra, memo, 7 August 2026

"Before we debate what predicts renewal, somebody needs to tell me whether we have been invoicing three customers for conversations a human touched. That is not a metrics question. Please do not send anything to the data room until I have an answer."

"With respect — the design doc said this. I asked whether assisted drafts should be counted for billing. Nobody answered. We had a release date."

"Our operations head at Shams does not look at resolution percentage. He looks at how many of his people he needs on Saturday during a promotion weekend. When we talk to him in his language, the renewal conversation takes ten minutes."

Cheryl Tan, in the APAC QBR debrief, 3 August 2026

"Whatever you decide, decide before the twentieth. I have a proposal out to a New Jersey logistics group with a resolution-rate commitment in it, and if the definition moves after they sign, that is my problem and then it is legal's problem."

Vikram Sethi, WhatsApp to Aditi, 9 August 2026, 21:40 IST

8. The options, as Aditi currently sees them

Option one: hold the line for one quarter. Keep day-60 auto-resolution as the governing proxy through the Series D, fix the definition quietly, add a footnote to the data room describing the January 2025 change, and revisit the metric in January 2027. The case for it is that the evidence against the proxy is a single twelve-month read on one cohort, that the company has nine weeks of fundraising ahead, and that an organisation which repudiates its central metric in August cannot explain itself in September. The case against is that the roadmap being funded by that round is built on the proxy, and another two quarters of building toward it is two quarters of possibly-wasted engineering.

Option two: replace the threshold with a composite quality metric. Define a "healthy resolution" — resolved without human involvement, no re-contact in 48 hours, CSAT at or above 4, no escalation re-work — and govern on that. It is legible, it closes the gaming routes that intent sprints and aggressive deflection exploit, and it aligns with what Lukas's interviews report. Against it: three of its four components are instrumented inconsistently or only since March 2026, CSAT methodology varies by account, and the metric would fall by perhaps twenty points overnight, which is an awkward thing to put in a data room.

Option three: adopt Ritika's index. Move renewal forecasting and roadmap prioritisation onto the composite index, keeping resolution rate purely as a billing term. It predicts best and is hardest to game. Against it: no squad can reason about it, it cannot legally be computed for eleven accounts, its training data excludes the accounts that churned earliest, and Cheryl's team would lose the one number that gives them traction in customer conversations.

What Aditi had written at the top of her sheet, and then crossed out, and then written again, was a fourth line: Is the question which proxy, or is the question why we have one number doing four jobs? Below it she had written the names of the four jobs — quality target, renewal predictor, engineering OKR, invoice line — and drawn a box around the last one.

She had also noticed, and not yet told anyone, that Exhibit 4 does not support Option two as cleanly as it appears to. Shams Retail, expanding, sits at 81 per cent current resolution with low re-work. The Gurugram D2C brand, which downgraded, sits at 86 per cent with 38 per cent re-work. Insurer B, expanding, sits at 58 per cent with 9 per cent re-work. Three accounts, three different stories, and a sample of twelve from which one could construct a defence of any of the three options.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The data room must be finalised by Wednesday, 12 August, for the Thursday board call. The Series D term sheet is expected in October; Vivarta has fourteen months of runway at current burn and would have twenty-six with the round. Vikram's New Jersey proposal closes on 20 August and contains an unreviewed resolution-rate commitment. Shalini will not release finance sign-off on any external document until the contract exposure on the three outcome-priced accounts — plausibly ₹0, plausibly ₹3.8 crore — has been read line by line, which her team estimates will take three weeks.

Engineering capacity for the September–December period is eleven squads. Instrumenting escalation re-work across all 143 enterprise accounts, rather than the sampled 400 conversations, is estimated at 1.5 squads for a quarter. Building consent and contractual basis for Ritika's index across the eleven restricted accounts is a legal and customer-communication exercise that Vivarta's counsel estimates at two to four months under the DPDP framework, with no guarantee that all eleven will agree. Shams Retail's contract, which is governed by Dubai law and renews in March 2027, contains a service-credit clause tied to reported automation levels; Cheryl believes, but has not confirmed, that it references the dashboard definition rather than the billing one.

Ram's position on timing was stated in one line on Friday: "Nothing goes in the data room that we have to take out." Aditi read it twice on Sunday night and could not decide whether it was an instruction to disclose everything or to disclose nothing.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What precisely did Vivarta's 2023 analysis establish, and what did the company subsequently treat it as having established? Name the gap between those two things.

2. Exhibits 1 and 2 appear to contradict each other. List every reason the two charts might differ that has nothing to do with the proxy losing its validity, and say what evidence would be needed to rule each one out.

3. Cheryl's intent sprints and Tanmay's attribution change both raised the reported metric. Are they the same kind of problem? What does your answer imply about who is accountable for a metric's integrity in a company where four functions depend on it?

4. Exhibit 4 contains twelve accounts and supports at least three incompatible conclusions. Construct the strongest version of each, and then say what an analyst should do when a sample is simultaneously the best evidence available and too small to decide anything.

5. Vivarta's pricing has made a product metric into an invoice line. Was the October 2023 decision a mistake, or a reasonable trade whose cost is only now being paid? What would a company have to put in place at the moment it adopts outcome pricing to avoid arriving where Vivarta has arrived?

6. It is Monday morning, 10 August 2026, and Aditi has one hour with Ram. What does she do first, what does she commit to, and what exactly does she propose the board be told on Thursday — including what she would say if a director asks whether the 94 per cent figure in last year's deck was accurate?

It was nearly one in the morning when Aditi closed the laptop. The two charts were still open behind it. She had written three versions of an opening sentence for the Monday meeting and deleted all of them; the first sounded like a confession, the second like a cover-up, and the third like a request for permission she was not sure she should be asking for. Outside, the first of the pre-monsoon rain had started on the balcony. In Toronto it was mid-afternoon and Ritika was online. In Berlin, Lukas had sent a fourth link to the interview transcripts. Aditi did not open either message.

Proxies for Long-Term Value

What can we measure this week that predicts next year?

A board meeting in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March 2025, Meher Anand stood in front of Ojasvi Fit's board with a slide she did not like. Ojasvi Fit was a Bengaluru-based subscription fitness app — live and on-demand yoga, strength and mobility classes — with 140,000 paying subscribers and roughly ₹15 crore in monthly recurring revenue. The board's mandate for the next funding round was blunt: show a credible path to ₹500 crore in annual recurring revenue within three years. The one number that would actually settle the question — what fraction of a new cohort was still paying twelve months after joining — was true only for subscribers who had joined at least a year earlier. Anyone who had signed up after March 2024 was, by definition, still unmeasured.

This was the crux for Meher, as VP of Product: she needed a number she could look at this month that told her something true about a subscriber's fate a year from now. Pick the wrong number, and the company would spend the next four quarters optimising onboarding, pricing and content against a metric that felt like progress but predicted nothing — discovering the mistake only when the twelve-month cohorts finally reported in.

The idea, defined precisely

A proxy for long-term value is a metric observable soon after a customer's first interaction with a product that reliably predicts a business outcome — usually retention or revenue — that can only be measured much later. The word "reliably" is doing the real work in that sentence: a proxy is not simply any number that happens to be available early. It is a number whose relationship to the distant outcome has been checked against historical data and holds up.

The problem this idea was invented to solve is a timing mismatch. The outcomes a business actually cares about — will this subscriber still be paying in a year, will this cohort's spend grow or shrink — arrive on a calendar the business does not control, while product decisions need to be made weekly or monthly. Waiting for the true outcome before adjusting course means every decision is made roughly a year too late. The lineage runs through the balanced-scorecard work of Robert Kaplan and David Norton in the early 1990s, who popularised leading and lagging indicators in management generally, and through consumer-internet growth practice in the 2010s — Facebook's early finding that new users who added seven friends within ten days were dramatically more likely to stay is the best-known ancestor of this exact idea applied to software products. The single sentence Meher could say in that board meeting without sounding glib was this: a good proxy is a short-term number you can move this month that reliably predicts a long-term outcome you cannot measure for a year.

Figure 1. A proxy bridges an early, actionable signal to a distant outcome — and the bridge must be re-checked, not built once and trusted forever.

How it actually works

Practitioners who use this well follow a sequence that is mostly invisible in casual talk about "leading indicators," but each step matters. First, define the lagging outcome with precision — not "engagement" but a specific number, such as twelve-month gross revenue retention: the share of a cohort's starting MRR still present twelve months later. Second, generate candidate short-term signals from subscriber behaviour in the first days or weeks — session counts, feature adoption, a completed onboarding step. Third, and this is the step most often skipped, go back through historical cohorts that have already reached the twelve-month mark and check whether the candidate signal, measured early, actually separated subscribers who stayed from subscribers who left. A correlation confirmed on real, matured cohorts is a validated proxy; a plausible-sounding early metric never checked against real outcomes is a guess wearing a lab coat.

Fourth, convert the validated signal into an actionable threshold — not "more sessions are better" but "three or more classes in the first fourteen days." Fifth, give the proxy an owner, a reporting cadence and a named decision it feeds — a metric nobody is accountable for is decoration, not a proxy. Sixth, and this is the step teams forget most expensively: revalidate. A proxy is a statistical relationship measured at a point in time, inside a specific product. When the product changes — a redesign, a pricing change, a new content type — the relationship can weaken or invert even while the proxy number itself keeps climbing. Treating a proxy as permanent truth rather than a model with a shelf life is the most common failure mode covered later in this page.

The worked example: Ojasvi Fit's two cohorts

Meher's team had exactly the historical data this method needs. Ojasvi Fit had matured cohorts from January 2023 — subscribers whose fate at month twelve was already known — and could split them by how many workout sessions each subscriber logged in their first fourteen days.

28 + 66 + 103 + 63 = 260 retained subscribers out of 1,000, a blended twelve-month retention of 26.0% — matching the company's known aggregate for that cohort. The step from "0–1 sessions" to "9+ sessions" moves predicted retention from 8% to 63%, a spread wide enough to act on.

That table told Meher something specific and usable: whatever caused a new subscriber to log nine or more sessions in the first two weeks was strongly associated with still being a paying customer a year later. The natural next move was to make "reach nine sessions in fourteen days" an onboarding target. Before doing that, her team ran the same cut on a more recent cohort — subscribers who joined in February 2024, one month after Ojasvi Fit shipped a redesign letting subscribers "attend" a class simply by opening an on-demand video, a session logged the same way whether they watched three minutes or the full forty.

Overall retention is essentially unchanged, 26.0% to 26.4%. But the top bucket's predictive power fell sharply, 63% to 45%, because "a session" no longer meant the same behaviour.

The aggregate number looked reassuring — retention had, if anything, ticked up slightly. But the proxy that mattered for decision-making had quietly weakened. Before the redesign, reaching nine sessions meant nine real workouts, a strong signal of the habit that drives renewal. After it, a subscriber could reach nine "sessions" by briefly opening several videos without completing one, so the threshold now mixed genuinely engaged subscribers with casual browsers, and its correlation with staying a paying customer dropped accordingly. Had the growth team kept optimising toward "9+ sessions" on the old validation, they would have spent 2024's onboarding budget chasing a number that had stopped meaning what it used to mean.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Correlation is not the same as causation

A subscriber who logs nine sessions in two weeks might retain well not because the sessions caused their loyalty, but because both are downstream of the same underlying enthusiasm — a highly motivated joiner would likely have stayed regardless of what the product did. A proxy validated only by correlation tells you what to measure, not necessarily what to build; distinguishing the two usually requires an experiment, not just a cohort cut.

Proxies decay; Goodhart's warning applies

The economist Charles Goodhart observed in 1975 that a regularity used as a policy target tends to break down once it becomes the target — a relationship measured under one set of conditions is not guaranteed to survive once people optimise for it, or once the underlying system changes. Ojasvi Fit's redesign is a mild version of this: nobody gamed the metric, but the product changed what the metric meant. A proxy is a model, and models expire.

Leading indicator is not the same claim as validated proxy

Any metric that arrives early is technically a "leading indicator." Only some have actually been checked against a matured outcome and found to hold. Calling a plausible early number a proxy without running Table 1's exercise against real history is the most common shortcut teams take, and the most expensive one to discover late.

Validation needs enough matured cohorts to trust

Meher's exercise worked because Ojasvi Fit had cohorts old enough to have already reached month twelve. A company nine months old cannot validate a twelve-month proxy this way at all — a genuine constraint addressed in the next section, not a reason to skip the discipline.

A proxy is easily confused with a vanity metric

App opens and time-in-app rise and fall dramatically and feel like signal, but many have no demonstrated relationship to retention once actually checked against history. The test is not whether a number is easy to move; it is whether it has been shown, on matured cohorts, to predict the outcome that matters.

A proxy cannot tell you why

Even a well-validated proxy is descriptive, not explanatory. Knowing that nine sessions predicts retention does not tell Meher's team whether the mechanism is habit, instructor quality or something else — that needs further investigation, and building blindly toward the number risks manufacturing the metric without manufacturing the value.

Ask what changed before trusting a proxy again

Any pricing change, redesign or shift in who is signing up can silently move the relationship between a proxy and its outcome. A thoughtful newcomer's habit is to ask, before relying on any proxy: when was this last checked against a matured cohort, and has anything changed since?

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and company stage

At Ojasvi Fit, a consumer subscription business, the proxy lived in individual behaviour measured in days: sessions, class completions, a habit forming inside two weeks. Contrast that with Rakshan Cloud, a fictional Bengaluru B2B expense-management platform selling annual contracts to mid-sized enterprises. Its lagging outcome — contract renewal — arrives once a year, and the relevant proxy is organisational rather than individual: how many employees at a client activated their account in the first thirty days, and whether the finance team completed the accounting-system integration. A single champion logging in daily says little; broad adoption across a client's finance team says a great deal, because a renewal decision is made by a committee.

A two-sided marketplace complicates the picture further. Consider a fictional B2B agricultural marketplace, Nabha Trade Cloud, connecting grain traders to mill buyers. A buyer's repeat order within thirty days might predict future spend — but only if sellers keep enough stock listed to fulfil it. A proxy validated purely on buyer behaviour can quietly fail if seller-side liquidity deteriorates. Marketplace proxies generally need a matched pair, one for each side, plus a fill-rate check guarding against either side's proxy meaning less than it used to.

Company stage changes the exercise too. An early-stage company, without enough matured cohorts to run Meher's kind of table, has to borrow proxies validated at analogous companies and treat its own as provisional until enough history accumulates. A later-stage company like Ojasvi Fit, with years of matured cohorts, can validate rigorously on a fixed cadence — and, once it can afford it, hold out a control group entirely from the optimisation effort, a technique covered separately as long-term holdouts.

Common mistakes

Treating a moveable metric as a meaningful one. The symptom is a proxy climbing steadily while the true lagging outcome stays flat or worsens. The error is picking a number because a team can influence it, not because it predicts anything. The cheapest diagnostic: plot the proxy against the actual outcome on every matured cohort and look for the lines diverging.

Never revalidating after a product change. The symptom looks exactly like Ojasvi Fit's redesign: the proxy keeps rising while long-term value stays unmoved. The error is treating a validated relationship as permanent rather than a model with an expiry date. The cheapest diagnostic is a standing reminder — quarterly, or right after any redesign — to re-run the cohort cut.

Wiring a noisy proxy straight into a target. The symptom is a metric swinging sharply week to week, sending the roadmap lurching in response to sampling noise from a small cohort. The error is mistaking volatility for signal. The cheapest diagnostic is checking the sample size behind the number before anyone puts it in an OKR.

Optimising the proxy at the expense of the product. The symptom is the proxy improving while complaints or refunds quietly worsen. The error is forgetting the proxy is a means, not the end — a team can always inflate a number without creating real value. The cheapest diagnostic is pairing every proxy with a guardrail metric allowed to veto it.

What good looks like

Six weeks after the board meeting, Meher's team had a proxy they trusted enough to present with confidence: "three or more classes attended in the first twenty-one days," validated against Cohort A's matured history and flagged as provisional pending a fresh check on Cohort B once its twelve-month mark arrived. They named an owner — a growth product manager, not a dashboard — and set a quarterly review where the matured-cohort correlation would be checked again, redesign or no redesign. Crucially, they paired the proxy with a guardrail: median class-completion rate, so a subscriber hitting "three classes" by abandoning each one early would show up as a warning, not a win. The board slide did not claim certainty it did not have; it showed the correlation, the sample size behind it, and the date it was last checked.

What Meher decided, and what comes next

Meher recommended the board fund a redesigned onboarding flow built around getting new subscribers to three completed classes in three weeks, with the completion-rate guardrail reported alongside it every quarter, and an explicit commitment to re-run the validation the moment any redesign touched how sessions were logged. The reasoning she gave was not that this proxy was certainly right, but that it was the most rigorously checked signal the company had, checked against real matured cohorts rather than intuition, and built with its own expiry date attached rather than presented as permanent truth.

The natural next step for a team at this point is long-term holdouts — deliberately withholding a slice of users from every proxy-driven optimisation effort so that, a year later, the company can check not just whether the proxy moved but whether moving it actually changed the real outcome. That is the discipline that turns a validated correlation into something closer to a causal claim.

Two questions worth sitting with:

What upstream product change could quietly break one of your team's proxies without anyone noticing until a matured cohort finally disagrees with it?

If your proxy and your actual long-term outcome ever pointed in different directions, which one would your organisation actually trust — and would that be the right call?

Proxies for Long-Term Value

Two companies, one problem: the number that decides the business arrives two years after the decision that determines it.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On Tuesday 14 April 2026, in a converted mill building in Lower Parel, Devika Rathore put a single slide in front of Avani Lending's risk committee. Avani was a five-year-old digital lender making small-ticket personal loans — median first ticket ₹28,000, 4.8 lakh borrowers on book, ₹1,340 crore disbursed in the preceding year, most of it through a co-lending arrangement with a mid-sized private bank. The co-lender's credit head had asked a reasonable question: on what evidence did Avani believe the borrowers it was acquiring in 2026 would be worth more over their lifetime than those it had acquired in 2024? Nobody would know until mid-2028. Contribution margin per acquired borrower — interest and fee income, less credit losses, servicing and acquisition cost — settled only about twenty-four months after acquisition, once second and third loans had either happened or not and the delinquency curve had flattened.

Devika, as Chief Product Officer, did not have twenty-four months. She had a quarterly roadmap and a growth budget, and needed a number visible at day ninety that said something trustworthy about rupees at month twenty-four.

Nine days later and 150 kilometres east, Rukmini Deshpande faced a structurally identical problem with a different shape. Chinar Work Cloud sold field-service management software to large Indian enterprises — utilities, elevator companies, diagnostic chains — on annual contracts averaging ₹38 lakh, with 310 live clients and ARR of ₹118 crore. Chinar's board had asked finance to commit to a net revenue retention figure for FY2028, a measure knowable at month twenty-four only for clients signed in 2024 or earlier. Rukmini's decisions for the coming year — a self-serve integration builder, heavier onboarding staffing, tying customer-success compensation to activation — all had to be made against a number that would not exist until they were two years old.

Both were reaching for the same instrument. Neither was certain it would hold.

2. The idea, and the argument inside it

A proxy for long-term value is a quantity observable soon after acquisition that stands in, for decision-making purposes, for a business outcome realisable only much later. The technical literature calls it a surrogate, which is the more honest word: a surrogate acts on behalf of an absent principal, and the whole question is how faithfully.

The intellectual history begins not in software but in clinical trials, where the problem is starkest: cardiovascular mortality takes a decade to measure and drug approvals cannot wait. In 1989 the biostatistician Ross Prentice set out the conditions a surrogate endpoint must satisfy to substitute for the true endpoint — it must be associated with the outcome, affected by the treatment, and must capture the treatment's entire effect, so that once you know the surrogate the treatment tells you nothing further. Seven years later Thomas Fleming and David DeMets wrote the sentence every product manager should have taped to a monitor: a correlate does not a surrogate make. They had the corpses to prove it — antiarrhythmic drugs suppressed the arrhythmias that correlated beautifully with cardiac death, and then killed more patients than placebo.

Two other lineages converge here. Charles Goodhart's 1975 observation — that a statistical regularity collapses once used as a policy target — and Donald Campbell's parallel law explain why surrogates rot under pressure; Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard (1992) gave management the leading-and-lagging vocabulary. And in 2019 Susan Athey, Raj Chetty, Guido Imbens and Hyunseung Kang formalised the surrogate index: rather than nominate one early metric, fit a model on historical data where both the early vector and the long-run outcome are observed, and use its prediction as the experimental endpoint.

Practitioners divide into three camps, and the division is real rather than rhetorical. The predictive camp, dominant in growth analytics, holds that a proxy's job is forecasting and segmentation. It will sign a proxy validated on matured cohorts is a legitimate instrument for forecasting and for allocating attention. It will not sign therefore, raising the proxy raises the outcome. The causal camp, descended from Prentice, holds that any metric used as a target must have been shown under randomisation to transmit the effect it claims to transmit. It will sign only causally validated surrogates may be optimised; it will not sign historical correlation is sufficient evidence to fund a roadmap. The portfolio camp, inheriting Goodhart and the scorecard tradition, argues that the search for the one true proxy is a category error: any single number made a target will be corrupted, so the answer is a small basket plus explicit guardrails. It will not sign that any single validated proxy is safe to hand to an incentivised organisation.

The disagreement is not about whether proxies work. It is about what a proxy licenses you to do: forecast, or act.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Rukmini's team began where most teams begin and also stop: with a cohort cut. Tanvi Iyer, Chinar's analytics lead in Hyderabad, took the 140 clients signed in FY2024 — all now past their twenty-fourth month — and bucketed them by the share of contracted seats that had logged a qualifying action within forty-five days of go-live.

Weighted: (34×71 + 41×89 + 39×112 + 26×138) ÷ 140 = 100.1%, which reconciles to Chinar's reported FY2024 cohort NRR. The spread from bottom to top bucket is 67 percentage points.

A 67-point spread is arresting, and it is exactly where unserious teams declare victory. Three further steps separate a validated proxy from an attractive table, and all three are usually left implicit.

The first is economic translation. Chinar's onboarding proposal would, on the team's own estimate, move roughly fifteen clients per cohort from the 25–49% bucket into the 50–74% bucket: (15 ÷ 140) × 23 percentage points = 2.46 points of cohort NRR, worth about ₹2.9 crore of recurring revenue against a ₹118 crore base. Stating it in rupees forces the second step, because ₹2.9 crore is now visibly comparable to the engineering it would cost.

The second is the causal fraction — the share of the bucket gap that would actually travel with a client you pushed across the boundary. Some of the 23-point gap reflects the activation; much of it reflects the kind of client who activates, one with an engaged sponsor and a real operational problem. If only 35% is transmissible, ₹2.9 crore becomes ₹1.0 crore and the trade looks different. Experts write this fraction down as an explicit assumption even when they cannot measure it, because the unwritten default is 1.0 and it is almost always wrong.

The third is the surrogate index rather than the single metric. Tanvi regressed 24-month NRR on three day-45 observables: seat activation share, whether the client's core-system integration was live, and support tickets per active seat. The fitted relationship, NRR ≈ 0.62 + 0.41 × activation + 0.18 × integration − 0.09 × tickets-per-seat, explained roughly 54% of the variance across those 140 clients — leaving 46% that three early numbers could not see. The index beat any single metric on two counts: it was harder to move cosmetically, since inflating activation while integration lagged and tickets rose produced little net movement, and it produced a predicted NRR with a standard error, which a threshold never does.

4. The conditions, stated as claims you can test

Four conditions determine whether this apparatus applies, and each can be checked rather than asserted. Claim one: enough cohorts have matured to see the relationship. Chinar passes narrowly — 140 clients is thin for four buckets, and the 26-client top bucket carries an interval wide enough that Tanvi refused to quote its 138% to two significant figures. Avani passes comfortably. Claim two: the product that generated the matured cohort is recognisably the product you sell today. Avani partly fails — its 2024 cohort predates a switch from monthly to weekly repayment options, which changes what an on-time payment means. Claim three: the proxy is movable by decisions you control. Both pass, and this is where danger enters, because movability is what makes a proxy corruptible. Claim four: the proxy is not trivially manufacturable. Chinar could inflate activation by auto-provisioning logins; Avani could inflate repeat borrowing with pre-approved top-ups. Absent a guardrail, both fail.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When the long-run outcome is dominated by factors outside the product — a lender's margin depends heavily on the rate cycle and on collections capacity — a product proxy looks uninformative or spuriously informative depending on the macro regime it was fit in. When the population changes faster than the proxy is revalidated, the historical relationship describes customers you no longer acquire. And when a surrogate fit on one mechanism is used to rank experiment arms working through a different one, it mis-ranks them systematically.

5. Hard edges

Two-sided markets break the single-proxy frame outright. Basera Rentals, a Pune marketplace for construction equipment, validated a buyer-side proxy — a second booking within forty-five days — on 2023 cohorts, where it predicted eighteen-month GMV per buyer reliably. In 2025 the proxy kept rising while eighteen-month GMV sagged, because the relationship had been fit in a period of abundant supply. Once utilisation on listed excavators crossed roughly 70%, a second booking stopped signalling a happy buyer and started signalling a lucky one. Marketplace proxies need a matched pair plus a liquidity condition under which the pair stays meaningful.

Regulated products face a stranger problem: the regulator has already chosen the proxy. Barkha Life Assurance reports thirteenth-month persistency to the IRDAI — simultaneously a genuine leading indicator of policy value and a number the distribution organisation is compensated against. The consequence is well known in the industry: lapses cluster immediately after the measured month. Where a regulator fixes the proxy, mature firms run a second, unpublished proxy internally and treat divergence between the two as the real signal.

Hardware plus software stretches the timeline. Chirayu Home Devices sells connected water purifiers on a consumables subscription; long-run value depends on filter replacement at months six, twelve and eighteen. Telemetry gives it an unusually good early proxy — litres dispensed in the first thirty days — but the replacement decision is also shaped by a service technician's visit, an event the product team does not instrument. The proxy is strong; the seam between product and field operations is where it leaks.

AI-native products face the sharpest version. Akaar AI, a Hyderabad contract-drafting assistant, watched its obvious proxy — suggestions accepted per document — rise 40% after a model upgrade while seat renewals did not move: the upgrade made suggestions longer, so fewer acceptances now covered the same work. The unit had silently changed. Expert practice in AI products is to define proxies in units of user-side work completed rather than model-side events emitted, because model-side events are redefined every time the model is replaced.

At the organisational seam, stated policy is quarterly revalidation. Observed behaviour is that proxies are revalidated when someone is embarrassed — a missed forecast, a churned marquee account — and that the revalidation is done by the team that owns the proxy, the team least motivated to discover it has decayed. Firms that manage this well separate validation from ownership, usually by placing validation in a central analytics function with no roadmap of its own.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A wide bucket spread is mostly selection. The tell is an enormous spread — Chinar's 67 points — alongside a small measured effect when the team actually runs an onboarding intervention. The obvious reading is that the proxy is powerful; the accurate one is that it is powerfully descriptive of customer type, and the transmissible share is a separate, much smaller quantity that must be measured rather than inferred.

Predictive accuracy and decision value are different properties. An expert notices when a proxy is highly predictive but immovable — a client's industry predicts NRR well and cannot be changed — and drops it from the target set while keeping it in the forecast. The naive move is to promote whatever correlates best, which fills the OKR sheet with demographics.

The threshold is usually a fiction the data does not support. "Three EMIs", "75% activation" — thresholds are chosen for communicability, while the underlying relationship is nearly always continuous. The tell is a team that cannot say what happens at 74%. Thresholds are defensible as operational targets, not as findings; treating a rounded cut-off as a discovered law is how a proxy acquires unearned authority.

Denominator drift beats numerator fraud. Teams guard the numerator against gaming; the commoner failure is the denominator quietly changing. Chinar's "contracted seats" began including read-only viewer licences in mid-2025, mechanically depressing activation share while no behaviour changed. The tell is a proxy that steps rather than drifts, on a date matching a release or a contract-template change.

Proxies are fit to a channel mix, not to a product. Avani's day-90 proxy was validated on a cohort acquired largely through a partner app. When paid social grew to a third of acquisition, the same behaviour meant something different, the underlying borrower differing in income stability. The expert re-runs the validation table split by channel before trusting the blended version.

The guardrail must be able to veto, not merely report. Most teams pair a proxy with a "watch metric" nobody has authority to act on. The tell is a quarter in which the guardrail deteriorated and the programme continued unchanged. A guardrail with no stopping rule is documentation of a failure, not prevention of one.

Revalidation is not re-running the same table. Competent practitioners re-cut the historical data annually. Experts also ask whether the outcome definition has drifted — whether "net revenue retention" still covers the same expansion products, whether contribution margin still nets the same collection costs. A proxy can be perfectly stable while the thing it proxies for is quietly redefined underneath it by finance.

Book proxy improvements at the causal fraction, not at face value. The tell is a planning document whose proxy-driven initiatives sum to a retention figure the company has never achieved. Experts discount every such forecast by an explicit transmissibility assumption, revisited after each holdout read.

7. Where the practice genuinely differs, and where it does not

The mechanics are the same everywhere; three things vary. The unit of observation: consumer products proxy on an individual in days, enterprise products on an account in weeks, and account-level proxies must aggregate behaviour without being dominated by a single enthusiastic champion — Chinar's activation share deliberately measures breadth, because a renewal is a committee decision. The latency gap: a consumer app may close the loop in ninety days and can afford lighter machinery, while Avani's twenty-four-month gap makes surrogate validity a board-level question. The corruption risk: where a human salesforce is compensated on the proxy, as in insurance distribution, Goodhart effects arrive within one incentive cycle; where the proxy is passive telemetry, decay comes from product change instead.

Stage matters more than most frameworks admit, and differently than expected. A seed-stage company cannot validate anything and should borrow a proxy while saying out loud that it is borrowed. A growth-stage company has matured cohorts and the strongest incentive to believe them uncritically, since the proxy is now in the fundraising deck. A late-stage company can afford holdouts and central validation; its real problem is organisational, with several teams each owning a conflicting proxy and nobody empowered to adjudicate. What does not differ, despite common claims, is the statistics — a B2B proxy is not conceptually different from a consumer one, merely smaller in N and longer in lag, which makes the same errors costlier rather than different in kind.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

The first is Chinar's, already laid out: a 67-point spread, translated to ₹2.9 crore, discounted by an assumed causal fraction of 0.35 to ₹1.0 crore, with an index explaining 54% of variance. Rukmini funded the onboarding work at the discounted number and asked Tanvi to hold out 20% of new FY2027 clients so the causal fraction could be measured rather than assumed. The second is Avani's validation, which produced an unusually clean economic picture.

The third case is what Avani did with that table, and it is the instructive failure. A ₹3,470 gap multiplied by any plausible lift in repeat rate produced numbers large enough to command attention. The growth team ran pre-approved top-up offers to on-time borrowers at day 75, and it worked on its own terms: in a randomised test across 20,000 borrowers, the day-90 repeat rate rose from 27% to 41%. Fourteen points is 2,800 additional repeat borrowers, and at ₹3,470 each the projected gain was roughly ₹97 lakh per cohort.

When the test cohort matured in mid-2026, Anand Seshadri's credit team read it out. The induced repeaters delivered a twenty-four-month margin of ₹1,150, not ₹4,310, against a counterfactual of ₹840 — a gain of ₹310 each, about ₹8.7 lakh in total. Nine percent of the projection. Worse, ninety-day delinquency on the induced second loans ran 2.4 times the organic rate, consuming part of even that, and drew an internal audit query about whether the offers sat comfortably with the RBI's digital lending guidelines on unsolicited credit limit enhancement.

The diagnosis was precisely Fleming and DeMets. Taking a second loan had never caused a borrower to be valuable; it had revealed a borrower with stable income and genuine recurring credit need. Manufacturing the act did not manufacture the borrower. The recovery had three parts: Avani redefined the proxy as a borrower-initiated repeat application within 120 days with no outbound offer in the preceding thirty — a definition its own marketing cannot produce; it attached a stopping rule, pausing the programme automatically if thirty-day-past-due on second loans exceeded 1.3 times the organic rate; and it carved a permanent 5% holdout excluded from all lifecycle marketing, paying a small revenue cost for an uncontaminated measurement.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Assuming full transmissibility. Early sign: a plan whose proxy-driven gains, summed, exceed any retention number the company has posted. Diagnostic: what causal fraction is this forecast assuming, and where is it written down? Caught late, the cost is a missed board commitment plus a year of engineering aimed at a number rather than a customer.

Silent redefinition. Early sign: a step change on a date matching a release, a contract template or a model upgrade. Diagnostic: has the event, the denominator or the unit changed since the last validation? Late detection costs a full cohort of misdirected onboarding, as Akaar AI's acceptance-rate episode showed.

Validation owned by the optimiser. Early sign: the revalidation memo is written by the team compensated on the proxy and always concludes it still holds. Diagnostic: who last tried to falsify this proxy? The late cost is structural — an organisation that has lost the ability to notice it is wrong.

Population drift. Early sign: the proxy is stable while the acquisition mix moves. Diagnostic: does the relationship hold split by channel, geography and ticket size? Late, the company finds its whole playbook was fit to a customer it no longer acquires.

Guardrail without teeth. Early sign: a guardrail deteriorating two quarters running with no decision attached. Diagnostic: what number, at what level, stops this programme automatically? Late detection costs reputation and regulatory standing before it costs money.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether correlational validation is ever sufficient for a target. The causal position, steelmanned: the Prentice conditions are almost never satisfied in practice, the cardiology literature contains lethal counterexamples, and Avani's ₹8.7 lakh against ₹97 lakh is the same pathology in rupees; no proxy should be made a target without a holdout. It rests on strong evidence and one assumption — that holdouts are affordable. It would be wrong if the cost of a year-long holdout in forgone learning velocity exceeded the expected loss from acting on a merely correlational proxy, which at an early-stage company it plausibly does.

The second is single metric versus index. The index position: a fitted index uses more information, resists cosmetic gaming, and carries an honest standard error. The single-metric position, steelmanned: a proxy's job is partly social — it must be understood, remembered and argued with by people who will never see the regression — and a model nobody can interrogate becomes an oracle, refit by the same team whose work it grades. This would be wrong if organisations acted on model outputs as rigorously as on simple thresholds, which most product organisations demonstrably do not.

The third, least settled, is whether proxies should be optimised at all or merely monitored. The monitoring position holds that the only legitimate targets are outcomes the customer experiences directly — a completed job, a repaid loan — and that proxies belong in forecasting and triage, never in OKRs. Its opponents call this a counsel of perfection: quarterly planning requires quarterly targets, and refusing to set them does not produce patience, it produces worse targets chosen informally. Nobody here has decisive evidence, because the experiment that would settle it cannot be run.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces the validation table. Someone who has internalised it produces the table and immediately asks what would have to be true for it to be misleading, then goes looking for that. They quote proxy-driven forecasts with the transmissibility assumption in the same sentence. They can name the date their proxy was last validated and the release that would most plausibly have broken it. They separate the three uses of a proxy — forecast, triage, target — and apply a visibly higher bar to the third. And they treat a proxy's authority as expiring rather than accumulating: the longer a number has gone unchallenged, the more suspicious of it they become, which is the opposite of how organisations naturally behave.

12. What each of them decided

Rukmini Deshpande funded the onboarding investment at ₹1.0 crore rather than ₹2.9 crore, moved the surrogate index into Chinar's forecasting process while keeping a single legible activation threshold as the team's operating target, and — the decision that mattered most — moved revalidation out of her own organisation into central analytics, with a standing instruction to refit the index annually and after any change to contract templates or seat definitions. She told the board that Chinar's FY2028 NRR commitment carried a causal-fraction assumption, and named it.

Devika Rathore's decision followed a loss and was harder. She kept the proxy, concluding that the day-90 signal was genuinely informative about borrower quality and that the error had been in treating a revelation as a lever. Avani now uses it to underwrite and forecast, and targets only the borrower-initiated version, behind the delinquency stopping rule and the 5% holdout. The co-lender's credit head, shown the revised framework in July 2026, accepted it — not because the number was higher, but because it came with an account of how it could be wrong.

Discussion questions

1. Avani's campaign raised its validated proxy by fourteen points and destroyed value. Without a matured control group, how many more quarters would the company have spent congratulating itself — and what in the interim data could have tipped Devika off earlier?

2. Chinar's index explains 54% of the variance in twenty-four-month NRR. Is a proxy that leaves 46% unexplained a reasonable basis for a board commitment? What would you require alongside it?

3. Barkha Life's regulator has fixed the proxy its salesforce is paid against. Running product there, would you optimise the regulated number, the internal one, or refuse the framing — and what would you tell the distribution head?

13. Going deeper

Input vs output; leading vs lagging. The vocabulary this topic sits inside; a clean distinction stops teams calling every early number a proxy.

Choosing experiment metrics. Every experiment shorter than the outcome horizon uses a proxy implicitly; here the choice becomes explicit.

Long-term holdouts. The only instrument that measures the causal fraction rather than assuming it — the direct sequel to Avani's ₹8.7 lakh lesson.

What makes a good metric. Predictiveness is one property among several; here is the rest of the checklist a proxy must pass.

Vanity vs actionable metrics. Picking movable numbers over meaningful ones, treated head-on.

GAME framework. Ties goal, action, metric and evaluation together so a proxy arrives with an owner and a decision attached.

Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions. Locates which part of the value chain a proxy actually informs — usually assumed rather than checked.

Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio. The formal taxonomy of metric construction — and why Chinar's activation share behaves differently from an activation count.

North Star metric. Usually a proxy promoted to company-wide authority; study what that promotion does to its shelf life.

Vaanya Petcare: The Number That Governs the Quarter

Bengaluru, April 2026. A product leader must choose the short-horizon metric her company will use to decide what to build — before the long-horizon metric she actually cares about can possibly arrive.

1. The decision

At 7.40 on the morning of Tuesday, 21 April 2026, Meghna Rao took the lift to the fourth floor of Vaanya Petcare's office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru with a printed sheet she had annotated three times over the weekend. As vice-president of product, she had nine days before the FY27 quarterly planning offsite on 30 April, and one thing to settle before it: which single early metric Vaanya would use to decide whether an experiment had worked.

The company's board governed on twelve-month gross profit per acquired customer, which stood at ₹5,900 against an acquisition cost of ₹1,620. Meghna's four squads shipped roughly eleven experiments a quarter. Eleven decisions a quarter cannot be taken with a number that arrives a year in arrears, and Vaanya had been taking them, for two years, on thirty-day repeat-purchase rate — a metric that nobody had validated and everybody quoted.

Her chief executive, Devika Sundaram, had made the stakes explicit in March: the FY27 plan committed Vaanya to spending ₹34 crore on acquisition. "Whatever number you pick," Devika had said, "it will decide what four squads build for a year, and it will decide which customers marketing goes after. Pick carefully, and be able to defend it."

2. The company

Vaanya Petcare was founded in 2021 by Devika Sundaram and a veterinarian, Dr Aravind Pillai, on a simple observation: India's urban pet population was growing fast, and owners were feeding dogs a mixture of leftovers and imported kibble with little guidance. Vaanya sold a subscription to fresh, gently cooked meals portioned to a specific dog — weight, breed, age, activity level — delivered weekly in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Mumbai, Delhi NCR and Chennai, with treats, supplements and a teleconsult service alongside.

By March 2026 it had about 78,000 active subscribers, average monthly billing of ₹2,350, blended gross margin of 38 per cent and FY26 revenue of ₹104 crore. Subscriptions were billed on UPI Autopay mandates through a Razorpay integration, with cards as a fallback. Its competitive neighbourhood was crowded and respectable: Heads Up For Tails and Supertails in premium pet commerce, Drools and Farmina on shelves, Amazon and Flipkart for everything, and Zepto and Swiggy Instamart increasingly capturing impulse treat purchases that Vaanya used to own. A pilot supply agreement with a Dubai retail group, signed in February 2026, promised a small export line for treats and supplements and had made the question of measurement suddenly harder, because Dubai customers would not be on UPI at all.

3. The situation

The immediate trigger was an experiment that had gone well and then gone strange. In October 2025 the payments squad, led from Pune, had shipped a smarter retry cascade for failed UPI mandate debits: retry timing tuned to salary-credit patterns, a WhatsApp nudge, and a one-tap re-authorisation. Thirty-day repeat-purchase rate rose 6.1 percentage points, the largest single movement Vaanya had ever recorded. The squad was congratulated. The growth team built the FY27 plan on the assumption that a further four points were available from the same territory.

In March 2026, Arjun Balakrishnan, Vaanya's data scientist in Toronto, delivered the first full read on the cohort acquired in the quarter after that shipment. Twelve-month gross profit per customer was up 1.2 per cent. The proxy had moved six points; the outcome had barely moved at all.

Arjun's memo, sent at 04:10 India time and read by Meghna over breakfast, made an uncomfortable argument. Repeat purchase within thirty days was largely a measurement of whether a mandate debit had succeeded, and mandate success was mostly a function of the customer's bank, their balance on billing day, and Vaanya's retry logic. Fixing the plumbing had converted customers who would have paid anyway into customers who paid on time. That was worth something. It was not worth what the proxy's cohort gap implied.

Priyanka Nair, the customer-success lead in Singapore, read the same memo differently. Her team had been arguing since 2024 that the customers who stayed were the ones who had spoken to a vet in their first month — the ones whose feeding plan had been corrected, whose dog's weight had actually changed. "The ones who never talk to us," she wrote in the thread, "churn in month four when the novelty of the fresh food wears off and the price feels high. You cannot see that in a mandate debit."

Lena Brückner, the designer in Berlin, added a third concern with a screenshot: in her research sessions, Indian subscribers spoke about the teleconsult as reassurance rather than as a service — several had booked one and not attended, and still spoke warmly about having the option. Whether a completed consult or merely the existence of one was doing the work was, she noted, not something the data could presently distinguish.

4. The people

Meghna Rao, VP Product, Bengaluru. Accountable for the FY27 roadmap. Wants a metric her squads can move deliberately and which she can defend to the board in eighteen months when the truth arrives.

Arjun Balakrishnan, data scientist, Toronto. Has built a composite index that predicts twelve-month gross profit from fourteen early behaviours and validates far better than any single metric. Wants it adopted as the experiment read-out. Concedes, when pressed, that he cannot explain to a squad what a 0.03 movement in the index means.

Priyanka Nair, customer-success lead, Singapore. Wants the completed teleconsult as the company's proxy, because it is the one behaviour her team can influence and because it matches everything she hears on calls. Her team's headcount case for FY27 rests on it.

Rohan Shetty, CFO, Bengaluru. Cares about CAC payback and is sceptical of any metric that cannot be tied to cash. Points out that the teleconsult costs Vaanya about ₹310 in vet time and that making it universal would cost ₹2.4 crore a year at current acquisition volumes.

6. The options

Option A — adopt the month-2 autopay success proxy. Highest separation, majority coverage, trivially instrumented, and already understood by everyone. The cost is that it is close to a restatement of retention rather than a guide to product work, it rewards payments and discounting work over product quality, and it is meaningless for the Dubai line, which will not run on UPI mandates.

Option B — adopt the completed teleconsult as the primary proxy. It is the only candidate with an interventional record: three experiments moved it and the outcome followed. It has a legible mechanism — a corrected feeding plan produces a visibly healthier dog. Its costs are coverage (17 per cent today), an unproven marginal effect at scale, ₹2.4 crore of vet time if made universal, and the risk that squads optimise for booked consults rather than useful ones.

Option C — adopt Arjun's composite index. The best predictor by a wide margin and the most resistant to any single form of gaming. The costs are opacity — no squad can reason about what moves it — the political difficulty of a metric only one person in Toronto can recompute, and the fact that its validation rests on the same historical cohorts whose product no longer exists in the same form.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Why do Exhibits 1 and 2 rank the candidate proxies differently, and which ranking should govern a decision about what to build next quarter?

2. What exactly did the retry-cascade experiment prove, and what did Vaanya wrongly conclude from it?

3. If Vaanya adopts the teleconsult proxy, what is the cheapest way a squad could raise it by ten points without creating any value — and what guardrail closes that route?

4. Which option should Meghna take to the 30 April offsite, and what would she need to commit to so that the company can discover, within a year, that she was wrong?

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is the difference between a metric that predicts long-term value across customers and one that acts as a valid surrogate for the effect of a decision. Exhibit 1 tests only the first property. Exhibit 2 tests the second, and it is the harder and more useful test: it asks whether, when the company intervened, the proxy's movement pointed the same way as the outcome's. A proxy that fails this test can be a perfect predictor and still send a roadmap in the wrong direction — which is what the Diwali bundle did, raising debit success while lowering twelve-month profit.

A well-reasoned answer will separate three things that Exhibit 1 blurs: separation (how far apart the two groups are), coverage (how much of the base the proxy can address), and movability (whether product work can shift it without destroying the mechanism). It will also notice that the autopay metric is so close to the outcome that it is nearly a leading restatement of it — useful as a health check, useless as a compass.

One defensible path. Meghna adopts the completed teleconsult as the primary decision proxy for FY27, on the strength of Exhibit 2 rather than Exhibit 1, and demotes month-2 autopay success to a guardrail that must not fall. She does not make consults universal on day one: she commits to a single properly powered experiment in May that offers the prompted free consult to a randomly selected half of new subscribers, so that the marginal effect — on the customers who would not have booked unprompted — is measured rather than inferred from the cohort gap in Exhibit 1. She adds a quality guardrail (consult duration and a post-consult plan change) so that squads cannot win by booking consults nobody attends, which is precisely the failure Lena's research foreshadowed. Arjun's index is adopted as a secondary read-out reported alongside every experiment, on the argument that it costs nothing to observe and will earn trust or lose it over four quarters. Finally, she carves out a 2 per cent holdout from all FY27 product changes and schedules its twelve-month read for May 2027, so the company has an instrument that can contradict her.

The reasoning is that a proxy's job is to guide decisions, not to describe customers; that the only evidence bearing on that job is interventional; and that any proxy adopted in April 2026 should be assumed to have an expiry date, especially in a company about to start selling in a market where its best-separating metric does not exist.

Vanity vs Actionable Metrics: Is This Number Changing Decisions, or Just Going Up?

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Farak Money, a Pune-based savings and micro-investing app, sat in a pre-board rehearsal with two slides open. One said the company had crossed 42 lakh cumulative downloads and 28 lakh registered users, up 35 percent year on year. The other, which she had built herself and not yet shown anyone, said that the number of customers who actually completed a savings transaction in a given week had been stuck at roughly 1.4 lakh for two straight quarters. The board meeting was four days away, Farak Money was mid-way through a Series C raise, and the CEO wanted the first slide on page one of the deck.

The tension was not cosmetic. Farak Money had spent ₹3.2 crore on performance marketing that quarter, much of it on video ads timed around cricket season, and downloads had jumped 38 percent quarter on quarter. Registrations followed. But Ananya's dashboard, built with her data lead in Bengaluru, showed that most people who downloaded the app never completed the one action the business model depended on: an automatic weekly round-up transfer into a savings goal. If the board approved another ₹5 crore of the same spend, Farak Money would buy more of exactly the users it already had too many of, and the metric that predicted revenue would stay flat. Ananya's task before Thursday was to decide which number to defend, and to explain, arithmetically, why.

The Idea

A vanity metric is any number that reliably goes up, is easy to report, and does not, by itself, tell anyone what to do differently. An actionable metric is tied to a specific, repeatable decision: if it moves, someone changes a plan. The distinction was named and popularised by Eric Ries in his 2011 book The Lean Startup, as part of what he called innovation accounting — a discipline for judging whether a young company is actually learning, rather than producing charts that trend upward. Ries was reacting to a failure he had watched repeatedly in Silicon Valley: founders raising a round on total signups or page views, numbers that always climb as long as marketing spend continues, while the underlying business made no real progress. The idea travelled into product management because the same failure recurs anywhere a team can spend money to inflate a top-of-funnel number.

The one sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: a metric only earns a place in a decision meeting if someone can say, in advance, what action a change in it would trigger. Total downloads fails that test, because no one at Farak Money would change the marketing or product roadmap based on downloads alone — they would first ask what happened to those users afterward. Weekly active savers passes, because a fall in that number has one clear owner, one clear review cadence, and one clear next step: fix activation or retention before spending more to acquire.

How It Actually Works

Distinguishing a vanity metric from an actionable one is a five-step discipline, and most people who use the vocabulary loosely skip the last two steps. First, name the decision the metric is meant to serve — the actual choice, such as "increase or pause paid acquisition spend." Second, ask whether it is a rate rather than a cumulative count; counts such as total downloads can only ever increase, so they cannot fall to warn of a problem, while a rate such as "share of new registrants who complete a savings transaction within seven days" carries information both ways. Third, check comparability across time and cohorts — a number that changes definition, or mixes a marketing-driven spike cohort with an organic one, cannot support a decision. Fourth, assign an owner and a cadence: a metric nobody checks weekly or monthly is acted on by no one, however good it looks in a deck. Fifth — the step most often skipped — pressure-test whether the metric can be inflated without the business improving; if a team can move it through means a customer would never notice, such as buying downloads that never activate, it is gameable and untrustworthy, even if true.

Applied to Farak Money, the cumulative counts — downloads, registrations, assets under management — fail steps two and five: they are counts, not rates, and marketing spend alone can move them. Ananya's candidate metric, weekly active savers with at least one completed auto-save in a rolling four-week retained cohort, passes all five: a rate, comparable cohort to cohort, owned jointly by growth and product on a monthly cadence, and immune to ad spend alone, since spend only feeds the top of the funnel, not the middle.

A Worked Example

Ananya's data lead in Bengaluru pulled Q2 numbers to make the argument concrete. The figure and table below walk through the same funnel twice: once with actual Q2 numbers, once with a single input changed, to show which lever moves the metric that matters.

Read the funnel as Ananya read it in rehearsal. Of 9,80,000 downloads, 42 percent completed KYC and registered — 4,11,600 people. Of those, only 18 percent activated with a first automatic save within seven days — 74,088 people. Of that activated group, 55 percent were still saving in week four — 40,748 newly retained savers. Against that, the existing base was already churning at roughly 3.5 percent a week, removing close to 19,300 people over the quarter. Net, the base of 1,38,000 weekly active savers grew to only about 1,40,000 — shown to the board as "flat" — despite a 38 percent jump in downloads and ₹3.2 crore of fresh spend. The vanity metric moved sharply; the actionable one barely moved.
