Holding downloads and registration constant and improving only first-save activation — from 18 to 30 percent, a redesign her team had already prototyped — pushes the retained base up by a third, to roughly 1,86,600, with no additional rupee of spend. This is the argument Ananya intended to make: the lever that moves the metric the business depends on sits in the middle of the funnel, in activation, not at the top, in acquisition.

The Nuances

A metric can be actionable for one team and vanity for another

Total downloads is a legitimate input to the App Store Optimization team's keyword-bidding decision. It becomes a vanity metric only when presented as a proxy for business health to an audience that will use it to decide something it cannot predict, such as revenue growth.

Absolute numbers hide rate changes

Farak Money's registered-user count will rise every month regardless of product quality, since almost nothing removes a person from "ever registered." The question to ask is always what the number is a share of, and whether that share is improving.

Vanity metrics are not always dishonest

Nobody at Farak Money fabricated the download figure. The distinction is about decision-relevance, not truthfulness — an accurate number can still tell you nothing about what to do next, which is more dangerous than a lie, because it survives audits.

Actionability depends on a pre-committed action

A metric only counts as actionable if the team can state, before seeing it, what they will do if it rises or falls. If leadership would spend the same regardless of what weekly active savers did, the metric is actionable in name only.

Gameability is a matter of degree, not kind

Even weekly active savers can be nudged by loosening "save" to a token ₹1 transfer. The newcomer's question should be: what is the cheapest way a team under pressure could move this number without helping a real customer?

A good metric still cannot tell you why

Knowing activation sits at 18 percent tells Ananya where to look, not what is broken — poor onboarding copy, a confusing KYC step, or mismatched ad creative are all consistent with it. Actionable metrics point at a location, not a diagnosis.

Context can convert a vanity metric into an actionable one

Total downloads becomes actionable once paired with a pre-agreed rule — "pause this campaign if cost per download exceeds ₹85." The label depends on the decision structure around the metric, not the metric alone.

Consumer, B2B, Marketplace — and Early vs Late Stage

In a consumer product like Farak Money, the vanity trap sits at the top of the funnel — downloads, registrations, app opens — because performance marketing can move these directly and cheaply. In B2B, the equivalent is "logos signed" or "seats provisioned," which a sales-led organisation can inflate through discounting without changing whether the product is used; the actionable equivalent is a usage-depth metric tied to renewal, such as the share of seats with a login in the last fourteen days. In a marketplace, the trap is subtler: gross merchandise value can rise because a few large sellers or buyers are subsidised into volume, while repeat transaction rate on both sides, unassisted by discounts, stays flat. Farak Money's rival, Ekanya Wealth, ran into exactly this in 2025, reporting asset growth that later proved concentrated in fewer than two hundred large depositors, a fact that surfaced only when a compliance review asked for concentration data.

Stage matters too. An early-stage team with thirty customers can justify treating a noisy but genuinely leading signal — interview sentiment, say — as temporarily actionable, since it has no larger sample to lean on. A company at Farak Money's stage, allocating real capital against the reported number, no longer has that excuse: the bar for "actionable" rises with the size of the decision it informs.

Common Mistakes

The first mistake is reporting a cumulative count as a rate — the symptom is a chart that only ever slopes upward, and the diagnostic is asking whether the metric could, in principle, fall next month. The second is choosing a metric because it is easy to instrument rather than decision-relevant — the symptom is a dashboard nobody cites in planning meetings. The third is conflating correlation with the driver, such as assuming app-open frequency causes retention when both trace to notification volume — caught only by a holdout group. The fourth is proliferation — forty numbers on one dashboard, none owned — the diagnostic is asking each owner what they would do differently if their number moved ten percent.

What Good Looks Like

At a comparable savings app, Devranga Finserv, the product lead had faced the same board pressure a year earlier and resolved it by presenting both numbers side by side, with the second framed as the one the company would be held to. Downloads and registrations were shown, honestly, as evidence the brand was working; weekly active savers, broken into activation and retention rate rather than one blended number, was shown as the metric the next quarter's spend would follow. The board approved a smaller, phased increase contingent on activation crossing 25 percent, and asked for the same funnel table next quarter rather than a fresh set of headline numbers. The business did not change instantly, but the decision structure around the metric did — which is the point.

Closing

Ananya presented both slides. She did not hide the download number — that would have been its own credibility problem — but opened with the funnel table, framed the flat weekly-active-savers base as the reason the next tranche of spend should go to onboarding redesign rather than more advertising, and asked the board to approve a smaller, activation-linked budget instead of the CEO's original ask. The board agreed to revisit the larger spend once activation crossed 25 percent, the threshold her arithmetic had shown would move the retained base by roughly a third. What she had actually changed was not the number itself but what the room was allowed to do with it.

The next idea worth studying from here is the metrics tree — decomposing a single north-star number into the multiplicative chain of rates that produced it, so an organisation can see which owned rate to push rather than argue over which headline number to report. Farak Money's funnel in Figure 1 is an informal version of that structure.

Two questions to sit with:

1. Name a metric you currently report upward at your own organisation. If it rose ten percent next month, would any specific person change any specific plan — and can you say now what that plan would be?

2. Which of your team's current metrics could be improved by a competitor spending money on something a customer would never notice or value? What would it take to make that path more expensive than actually improving the product?

Vanity and Actionable Metrics: the arithmetic of a number that changes nothing

On 6 August 2026, in a glass room off Chennai's Rajiv Gandhi Salai, Raghav Ananthakrishnan, Chief Product Officer of Nishaana Systems, was losing an argument he was technically winning. Nishaana sold warehouse-execution software to Indian retailers and logistics firms: thirty-eight enterprise accounts, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, 410 live warehouses from Bhiwandi to Hosur. The slide said monthly active warehouse users were up 41 percent year on year, at 62,800. Raghav's objection was that four accounts signed that year each mandated that every picker log in to a handheld device; the 41 percent was a contract clause, not a product achievement. The board member from the growth fund replied that the number was true. It was. What nobody could say was what to do with it.

He had a decision waiting. Engineering had scoped a Slotting Optimiser — software that reassigns storage locations nightly to shorten picker walking distance — at ₹1.2 crore, with the October release freeze nine weeks away. Renewals for the three largest accounts, ₹31 crore of ARR, fell due in March. If the optimiser moved picker productivity, finance valued the retained revenue at ₹3 crore in present terms. If not, the money was gone. Monthly active users would rise either way.

Five days later, Devika Bhatnagar, VP Product at Machaan Live in Bengaluru, faced the mirror image. Machaan was a live-commerce marketplace — creators streaming, viewers buying saris and skincare — with 4.3 lakh monthly buyers and ₹214 crore of annualised gross merchandise value. Its headline number for two years had been weekly active creators, just past 17,300, up 21.8 percent in a quarter. Devika knew why: partner operations, pressed by a Series B extension, had begun paying dormant creators a ₹200 stipend per stream. She had until end-August to propose the H2 objective, and the honest version would look like a step backwards.

2. The idea, and the people who disagree about it

A vanity metric is a number that is accurate, easy to report, and incapable of changing anyone's decision. An actionable metric is paired, in advance, with a decision: a threshold, an owner, a cadence, and a specific thing that happens if it moves. The vocabulary is Eric Ries's, from The Lean Startup (2011), where it sits inside innovation accounting; his test was that a metric be actionable, accessible and auditable. He was reacting to companies raising capital on cumulative signups and page views.

The lineage is older and less tidy than that framing suggests. Four schools are worth naming, because a practitioner who cannot tell them apart will misapply all of them.

The lean cohort school (Ries; Ash Maurya) holds that vanity is a property of the metric's shape. Cumulative counts can only rise, so they carry no warning; cohort rates carry information both ways. It will sign: a cumulative count should never be the primary number in a decision meeting. It will not sign: small samples make metrics useless — its method depends on reading twenty-customer cohorts.

The decision-theoretic school (Douglas Hubbard's How to Measure Anything, 2007, descending from the decision analysis of Raiffa and Howard) holds that vanity is not a property of a metric at all. A measurement has value only as it reduces uncertainty about a decision, and that value is computable as expected value of information. It will sign: actionability belongs to the pairing of metric and decision. It will not sign: downloads are inherently vanity. They are actionable to someone setting a bid cap, vanity to someone setting a roadmap.

The experimentation school (Ronny Kohavi, Diane Tang and Ya Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, 2020) holds that the binding constraint is statistical sensitivity. A metric you cannot move detectably inside one decision cycle cannot referee a product decision; hence the Overall Evaluation Criterion, a composite chosen for sensitivity and validated against long-term value. It will sign: a metric with no measurable minimum detectable effect at current traffic is not a decision instrument. It will not sign: an owner and a cadence make a metric actionable.

The incentive school descends from Charles Goodhart (1975), Donald Campbell (1979) and Marilyn Strathern's 1997 restatement: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Andy Grove's High Output Management (1983) supplies the remedy — paired indicators, where every quantity metric carries a quality counter-metric. It will sign: any target will be gamed, so the response is guardrails and rotation. It will not sign: there exists an inherently ungameable metric.

3. Mechanics: putting a rupee value on a number

Experts do something the textbook leaves implicit. They do not ask whether a metric is vanity; they ask what the organisation would do differently across each possible reading, and whether those actions differ. If the action is identical whatever the number says, the number is decoration. Hubbard's machinery makes this arithmetic rather than rhetoric.

Raghav ran that arithmetic on a Saturday morning. Frame the optimiser as a wager: build cost ₹1.2 crore, payoff if it lifts picker productivity and thereby renewal ₹3 crore, and an honest prior of 35 percent, informed by two earlier optimisation features that had underwhelmed. Expected value of building blind: 0.35 × 3.0 − 1.2 = −₹0.15 crore. The default is not to build.

Metric A was weekly opens of the existing slotting report. If slotting was genuinely a bottleneck, Raghav judged opens would read high about 70 percent of the time; if it was not, they would still read high about 60 percent of the time, because supervisors open reports out of habit. That small gap is the whole problem. A high reading occurs with probability 0.35(0.70) + 0.65(0.60) = 0.635, and the posterior is 0.245 / 0.635 = 38.6 percent, giving 0.386 × 3.0 − 1.2 = −₹0.04 crore. A low reading gives 28.8 percent and worse. The decision is the same in both branches, so the information value is zero. Metric A was still vanity.

Metric B was the share of live sites where a supervisor manually overrode the put-away suggestion at least once in fourteen days — diagnostic rather than descriptive, since overrides happen when slotting is visibly wrong to a person in the aisle. If slotting is a real bottleneck, Raghav put the chance of a high override rate at 85 percent; if not, 25 percent. A high reading then occurs with probability 0.46 and lifts the posterior to 64.7 percent, worth +₹0.74 crore. A low reading drops it to 9.7 percent. The branches diverge, so the metric is worth ₹0.34 crore against ₹6 lakh to instrument.

Two second-order effects follow, both usually left unsaid. First, a metric's value depends on the prior. Had Raghav's prior been 55 percent, building would have been positive without any measurement, and Metric B would also have been worth zero — not because it is bad but because the decision was already made. Metrics are worth most near indifference. Second, a ₹40 lakh data programme producing a metric worth ₹34 lakh destroys value.

Devika's constraint was different in kind: sensitivity. Machaan's honest business metric was repeat purchase within thirty days, at 6.2 percent. Detecting a 5 percent relative improvement means detecting 0.31 percentage points. At sixteen times the variance over the squared effect, that is 16 × 0.062 × 0.938 ÷ 0.0031², about 96,800 users per arm — essentially the whole eligible buyer base for a month, reading out thirty days after exposure. The proxy, add-to-cart during a stream, runs at 18.4 percent, needs 28,400 per arm, and reads out in a week.

This trade is where the two schools genuinely disagree, and it does not dissolve. The lean school would tell Devika to hold the line on repeat purchase and accept slow learning. The experimentation school would tell her to adopt add-to-cart and validate it as a surrogate, keeping a register of which experiments proxy and truth agreed on. Kohavi's caution is the sharp edge: surrogate validity is intervention-specific, and a proxy that tracked truth across eleven ranking tests can break on a twelfth that changes discounting.

4. When the distinction applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions can be stated as testable claims. One: the metric can fall. Nishaana's active-user count cannot while contracts mandate logins. Machaan's creator count can, so it passes — and still misled, which shows the condition is necessary, not sufficient. Two: a threshold and a consequent action exist before the reading. Metric B passed only because Raghav wrote down in advance that above 30 percent he would fund the build. Three: the cheapest path to moving it runs through customer value — Machaan's creator count fails at ₹200 a stream. Four: it is detectable inside one decision cycle. Five: it is comparable across periods and segments.

The distinction actively misleads in three situations. At very low sample sizes the count is the decision: a company with eleven enterprise customers should care that the twelfth signed, and a rate manufactures false precision. In regulated reporting, some cumulative counts are obligations rather than decision inputs — a lender filing disbursement volumes to the Reserve Bank of India is not making a vanity-metric error. And a brand metric nobody can act on this quarter may still be right to watch over three years.

5. Hard edges: seams, sides, silicon and models

Multi-product companies fail at aggregation before they fail at honesty. Nishaana's warehouse, transport and billing modules each have a defensible activity rate, but the company-level average is a weighted artefact nobody owns and nobody can move. The expert response is not a better composite but a refusal: report the three rates, never the blend.

Two-sided markets carry a structural vanity risk, because supply-side counts are the easiest thing in the business to buy. Machaan can manufacture creators; it cannot manufacture buyers who return. The disciplined formulation pairs each side's count with a productivity rate: creators, and GMV per streaming hour; buyers, and orders per buyer per month.

Hardware plus software produces the most persistent vanity metric in Indian industry, because distribution obscures it. Nihaar Instruments, a Pune maker of connected cold-chain sensors for pharmaceutical logistics, reported cumulative devices shipped — a number reflecting channel loading into distributors, not anything a customer had done.

AI-native products invert the usual reading of engagement. At Matsya AI, a Hyderabad firm selling an autonomous support agent, messages per conversation was celebrated until the team noticed that long conversations were the signature of a model failing to resolve an issue. Its replacement, resolution without human handoff, was gameable in the opposite direction — the agent could simply close tickets — and had to be paired with a seven-day reopen rate. Vanity metrics also survive longest at organisational seams, because the ratio spanning marketing and product has no single owner. Mature companies name one person accountable for each ratio, and most say they have long before they have.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Vanity is a property of a triple, not a number. The triple is metric, decision, audience. The expert's tell is that she will not judge a metric in the abstract; she asks who is in the room and what they are choosing between. The same slide can be rigorous in one meeting and negligent in the next.

The most dangerous vanity metrics were actionable last year. Metrics rot through definition drift and regime change. Nishaana's active-user metric was informative when every deployment was voluntary; it went hollow the day the first mandated-login contract was signed. The tell is that experts ask for a metric's definition history and treat an undated definition as a red flag.

Ratios can be vanity too. Practitioners learn that counts are suspect and rates virtuous, then meet a rate improved by shrinking its denominator — activation rising because the team stopped counting a low-intent channel. The tell is that experts display numerator and denominator separately, and are uncomfortable when shown a percentage alone.

Sensitivity must be measured, not assumed. A competent practitioner knows what a metric means; an expert knows its minimum detectable effect at current traffic, and therefore which debates the company can settle this quarter. Devika never proposed an experiment her sample could not resolve.

Surrogate validity is intervention-specific. The obvious reading is that a proxy either correlates with the outcome or does not. The expert reading is that the correlation holds within a class of interventions and breaks outside it. The tell is a maintained register of experiments recording where proxy and truth agreed, and a refusal to use the proxy outside it.

Every quantity metric needs a quality counter-metric. Grove's paired indicators remain the cheapest defence against Goodhart. Matsya's resolution rate is meaningless without reopen rate; Machaan's creator count without GMV per streaming hour. The tell is brutal: ask to see the guardrail. If nobody can name it in a sentence, the metric is already being gamed, intentionally or not.

Aggregation destroys actionability faster than dishonesty does. Mix shift can make a company-level rate move opposite to every segment inside it. The expert never reads a top-line rate without a decomposition, and has a standing rule about which dimension is always broken out.

A metric that never surprises anyone is dead. If a number has changed nobody's mind in four quarters it is ritual, however well constructed. The diagnostic is: when did this last cause us to do something different? Experts retire metrics for this reason; others keep them because removing a chart looks like hiding something.

Counts earn their place at low n. The blanket rule that counts are vanity is wrong at the beginning. With eleven customers the count carries nearly all the information and a rate carries noise. The expert states the threshold at which the company switches from counts to rates — and then actually switches.

7. Product type and company stage

The difference across product types is real but narrower than most treatments claim. In consumer products the trap sits at the top of the funnel, because paid acquisition moves it directly. In B2B and enterprise it sits at the contract boundary: seats provisioned, logos signed, users mandated in. The antidote is a usage-depth metric that survives the contract — at Nishaana, the share of warehouses where a supervisor changed a configuration in thirty days.

In platforms and marketplaces the trap is subsidy: any count on either side can be bought, and the tell is a productivity rate falling while the count rises. In hardware it is channel loading, as at Nihaar. In AI products it is the ambiguity of engagement, where cost per resolved task disciplines the conversation better than any behavioural rate.

Stage changes the bar rather than the principle. A seed-stage team with thirty customers may legitimately treat interview sentiment as its most actionable signal; a company allocating ₹1.2 crore against a reading cannot. The standard of evidence scales with the decision, and the common failure is a Series C company using seed-stage instruments.

8. Three worked examples

Nihaar Instruments: the gap between shipped and reporting. In January 2026 Nihaar's board deck showed 42,000 cumulative devices shipped and a software opportunity computed as 42,000 × ₹1,100 per device per year, or ₹4.62 crore. The operating reality was narrower at every step.

Nine thousand six hundred of 42,000 is 22.9 percent. Nihaar changed distributor margin to vest on commissioned-and-reporting rather than shipped. Over two quarters shipments fell from 18,000 to 11,000 — the headline number went down — while devices reporting weekly rose to 21,700 and paid subscriptions to 15,400, lifting software revenue to ₹1.69 crore.

Machaan Live: the mix-shift trap. In the same quarter, Machaan's checkout conversion appeared to improve from 2.57 percent to 3.57 percent, and the growth team claimed credit for a redesign. Both platform segments had in fact declined.

No number in the table is false; the blended rate is simply not a measurement of product quality, and reading it as one would have sent engineers to replicate a change that made things worse.

Navtaal Media: where the approach failed. Navtaal, a Delhi news application, did everything the literature recommends and still went wrong. It rejected cumulative downloads, chose a behavioural rate — daily sessions per active user — gave it an owner, a cadence and a threshold. Sessions rose from 3.1 to 5.4 over two quarters. The mechanism was notification volume, up from four to eleven pushes a day. Thirty-day retention fell from 34 percent to 27 percent, monthly actives from 18.0 lakh to 15.4 lakh, and subscription conversion stalled at 0.9 percent.

The recovery was neither fast nor free. Navtaal replaced the metric with days per week on which a reader reached sixty percent scroll depth on an article, and capped pushes at five a day. Sessions fell back to 3.6 and monthly actives stayed at 15.4 lakh, so the deck looked worse. But retention recovered to 33 percent and conversion rose to 1.6 percent — 24,640 subscribers at ₹149, or ₹36.7 lakh a month against ₹24.1 lakh before. Advertising fell about ₹8 lakh a month, leaving a net gain near ₹4.6 lakh and compounding. The vanity test, they learned, must be applied to the mechanism: they had asked whether the number could fall, never what the cheapest way to raise it would be.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The first failure mode is the mandated-usage metric, whose early sign is an activity number that steps up on contract start dates rather than drifting. The diagnostic is whether a customer could stop using the feature without breaching an agreement. Caught late, it costs a quarter's roadmap aimed at a bottleneck that was never there.

The second is the subsidised count, signalled by a count rising while per-unit productivity falls. The diagnostic is the marginal unit's contribution: Machaan's stipend bought 3,100 returning creators at ₹200 a stream across four weeks — ₹24.8 lakh a month — against roughly ₹50,000 of monthly take-rate revenue. Caught late, the subsidy becomes load-bearing in the fundraising narrative and cannot be withdrawn without a visible collapse.

The third is proxy drift, signalled by a widening gap between proxy and outcome in experiments where both are measured; the diagnostic is to recompute the correlation on the most recent twelve tests only. The fourth is proliferation — forty numbers, no owners — diagnosed by asking each owner what they would do differently at a ten percent move. The fifth is the unfalsifiable threshold, where targets are reset after the reading; its early sign is a target revised three times in a year, always in the direction the data went.

10. Where the disagreement is genuine

Four disputes remain open; a practitioner should be able to argue each side.

Is vanity a property of the metric or of the decision? The lean school's evidence is strong: cumulative counts and top-of-funnel volumes fail so reliably that treating them as categorically suspect is a good heuristic. The decision-theoretic school replies that shape is correlated with, but not identical to, zero information value — Metric A was a well-shaped rate worth nothing. The lean school is wrong if cumulative counts commonly carry decision value; the other is wrong if computing information value is so error-prone that the heuristic beats it.

Does ownership make a metric actionable, or does power? The metrics-tree tradition taught at most business schools says every metric needs an owner, a cadence and a decision. The experimentation school says this is necessary and badly insufficient, pointing to owned metrics no experiment can move detectably. The first position fails if teams routinely decide well on statistically inert metrics; the second fails if product decisions rarely turn on small effects.

Should cumulative counts ever be reported upward? The finance-led view says yes: they are the only numbers reconcilable to an audited statement, and they discipline a product organisation's taste for self-serving behavioural metrics. The product-led view says the audience will simply anchor on the larger, rising number. Neither has conceded.

Is the answer better metrics or better guardrails? The incentive school holds that metric selection is a losing game, since any target will be gamed, and effort belongs in paired indicators and rotation. Its opponents observe that rotation destroys the time series serious analysis depends on. Both costs are real; the trade-off is a judgement about how fast an organisation games things.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can classify metrics. Someone who has internalised it changes the decision structure rather than the slide. They write the threshold before the reading, knowing a target set afterwards is not a target. They can state the minimum detectable effect of every headline metric without looking it up. They will propose a metric that makes the company look worse, as Devika did, and defend it by what the organisation can now decide.

12. Closing

Raghav instrumented the override metric. It read 41 percent — above his pre-committed threshold of 30 percent — and he funded the Slotting Optimiser, presenting the information-value arithmetic rather than the activity chart. He also proposed retiring monthly active warehouse users in favour of configuration-change rate, and lost that argument for two quarters before winning it.

Devika proposed weekly active creators with at least ₹5,000 of unsubsidised gross merchandise value. Recomputed historically, the number was 8,900 rather than 17,300, and had been flat for three quarters. She took the reputational cost of showing it, and paired it with a productivity guardrail so the next incentive could not repeat the exercise. The stipend programme was wound down.

Discussion questions

1. Raghav's calculation rests on four probabilities he estimated himself. Does that make it rigorous or merely elaborate, and what would you require before letting it govern ₹1.2 crore?

2. Devika's proposed metric is harder to game but reads out more slowly and looks far worse. Under what circumstances is a board justified in rejecting a more honest metric in favour of a more legible one?

3. Navtaal's failure passed every standard vanity-metric test. What additional test would have caught it, and what does its absence from the standard checklist suggest about how the concept is usually taught?

13. Going deeper

What makes a good metric supplies the definition this topic negates: vanity metrics are the ones that fail its criteria. The GAME framework gives a structured route from goal to signal to metric, the step Raghav performed informally. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions locates each metric in the mechanism it belongs to. Direct versus proxy, magnitude versus ratio formalises the surrogate problem Devika faced. North Star metric covers how a headline number and its inputs are built; attention, transaction and productivity games explains Navtaal; and breadth × depth × frequency turns a flat usage number into three ownable rates.

Kirana Konnect: The Five-Lakh Slide

Is this metric changing decisions, or just going up?

1. Bengaluru, 26 September 2025

The budget lock was four days away. Meera Raghavan, vice-president of product at Kirana Konnect, had spent the morning of Friday the twenty-sixth in a meeting room on Old Airport Road looking at a single slide that her chief executive intended to open the Series C process with in the second week of October. It said, in large numerals, 4.62 lakh stores onboarded, and beneath it, 5 lakh by Diwali.

Diwali fell on 20 October that year. The gap was 38,000 stores in roughly three weeks, and the growth team in Pune had already told Meera how it would be closed: an extra ₹9.5 crore of field incentive, paid per store activated on the app, across Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Telangana. The money was available. The question in front of her, and the reason she had been asked to sign the quarter's product objectives by Tuesday the thirtieth, was whether stores onboarded should remain the number the company steered by at all.

2. Company background

Kirana Konnect was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 to solve an unglamorous problem: a neighbourhood kirana store owner in Nashik or Warangal ordered stock from eight distributors over WhatsApp and phone calls, kept accounts in a ledger, and had no way to compare prices. The company built an Android ordering app in nine Indian languages, connected it to regional distributors of staples, packaged foods and personal care, and took a margin on each order routed through it. By 2025 it operated in 190 cities, competed for the same retailers as Udaan and ElasticRun, sat alongside Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner and Metro Cash & Carry in the shopkeeper's decision set, and had begun listing sellers on ONDC.

Revenue in FY25 was ₹412 crore of gross merchandise value with a net take of ₹34 crore, against an operating loss of ₹61 crore. A second, smaller business had grown almost by accident: the ordering platform had been licensed as software to distributors outside India, the largest being a grocery distribution group in Dubai paying ₹1.8 crore a year, sold by a two-person team under Ravi Krishnamurthy in New Jersey. That business was 4 per cent of revenue and, because it was priced per connected retailer, gave the company its only contract in which the onboarding number was also the billing number.

3. The situation

The trouble had started with an ordinary question. In the third week of August, Rhea Fernandes, the company's data scientist in Toronto, had been asked to build a cohort view for the Series C data room. She pulled every store onboarded since April 2023 and asked a simple thing of the data: how many of them had placed an order in the last thirty days?

The answer was 1.71 lakh out of 4.62 lakh, or 37 per cent. Worse, the rate fell steeply by cohort. Stores onboarded in the first half of FY24, before the field incentive programme began, were ordering at 58 per cent. Stores onboarded during the FY25 festive push were ordering at 19 per cent. Fernandes sent the numbers at 4 a.m. India time with one sentence: "The denominator has been changing under us."

Nobody had falsified anything. The field executives were paid ₹180 per store that completed onboarding, defined as app installed, GST or shop licence captured, and one order placed. That definition had been written in 2023 and had worked. What it had not anticipated was that an executive could help a shopkeeper place a ₹400 order of two cartons of biscuits, collect the incentive, and never return. Roughly 44,000 stores in the FY25 cohort had placed exactly one order, ever.

Jia Hui Lim, who ran customer success from Singapore and covered both the Indian retailer helpline and the licensed international accounts, had been reporting something related for two quarters without being heard. Her weekly note described stores calling in confused about credit terms, and her Berlin-based designer colleague, Martin Weber, had redesigned the onboarding screens twice on the assumption that the drop-off was a usability problem. It was not obviously a usability problem. It was, as Weber put it on a call at an hour that suited neither Berlin nor Bengaluru, "a problem of who we are being paid to bring in".

4. The people

Vikram Nair, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants the five-lakh milestone before the Series C process opens. His argument is not vanity in the ordinary sense: he believes the number is the only thing an investor can compare across Udaan, ElasticRun and Kirana Konnect, and that a smaller, truer number will be read as a smaller company.

Sandeep Joshi, vice-president of growth, Pune. He runs 1,400 field executives across eleven states and their incentive structure. He wants the ₹9.5 crore and the existing definition. He points out, correctly, that his team hit every target it was given, and that changing the definition three weeks before Diwali would strand executives who had already made commitments to shopkeepers.

Rhea Fernandes, data scientist, Toronto. She wants the company to adopt monthly ordering stores as the headline and to publish it by cohort. She has no operational stake in the outcome and is the only person in the discussion whose incentive is unaffected either way.

Jia Hui Lim, customer-success lead, Singapore. She wants a single change: that any store counted as onboarded must have ordered in two separate weeks. She notes that the Dubai contract already works this way, because the client refused to pay for retailers who had merely installed the app.

Exhibit 1 is the document that made the argument unavoidable. Read across the second column, the company has grown every half-year. Read across the fourth and sixth columns, each successive cohort is less valuable than the one before it, and the festive cohort — the one bought with field incentives — is worth less than a third of the FY24 H1 cohort per ordering store. Exhibit 2 explains why the argument mattered financially rather than merely aesthetically. On cost per store, field incentive looked mid-table and the whole programme looked efficient at ₹985 a store. On cost per retained store, field incentive was the most expensive channel by a factor of two and a half, and the two referral channels — which together had absorbed only ₹3.5 crore — were the cheapest. The ₹9.5 crore proposed for the Diwali sprint was earmarked entirely for the most expensive column-six channel, because the target it was built to hit was measured in column three.

5. The options

Option A: hold the line and spend the ₹9.5 crore. Kirana Konnect reaches 5 lakh stores before Diwali, opens the Series C with a round number and a clean growth curve, and defers the definitional argument to the next financial year. The upside is fundraising momentum in a market where Udaan's scale is the reference point, and it keeps faith with 1,400 field executives mid-season. The cost is that the company spends its most expensive acquisition rupees on its least retentive channel, and that the data room will contain Exhibit 1, which a competent investor will ask for.

Option B: change the headline metric to monthly ordering stores, and re-cut the incentive. The company steers on 1.71 lakh ordering stores, reports it by cohort, and pays field executives on stores that order in two separate weeks within forty-five days, as Lim has proposed. The upside is that every rupee of growth spend becomes evaluable and the referral channels in Exhibit 2 get the budget on merit. The cost is immediate and visible: the headline number falls by nearly two-thirds overnight, the Series C narrative must be rebuilt in three weeks, and the executive incentive change lands in the middle of the festive season with commitments already made.

Option C: keep both, with a firewall. Stores onboarded stays as an external scale figure; monthly ordering stores becomes the internal steering metric and the sole basis of Q3 product and growth objectives. The ₹9.5 crore is split — ₹3 crore to the existing field push to honour commitments, ₹6.5 crore redirected to the referral channels — and the incentive definition changes from 1 November rather than immediately. The upside is that it avoids both the fundraising shock and the mid-season disruption. The cost is that firewalls leak: the number that appears in the investor deck has a way of reappearing in the planning document, and Joshi's team will continue to be measured, in practice, by whichever number the chief executive quotes.

6. Questions for discussion

1. What decision, specifically, would Kirana Konnect make differently if stores onboarded were 4.2 lakh instead of 4.62 lakh? What would it do differently if monthly ordering stores fell from 1.71 lakh to 1.5 lakh?

2. Exhibit 2 ranks the four channels in opposite orders depending on the denominator. Which ranking should govern the ₹9.5 crore, and what would you need to believe for the other one to be right?

3. Nair argues that a comparable number is worth more to the Series C than an accurate one. Is he wrong, and if he is only partly wrong, what exactly is the part he is right about?

4. It is Tuesday the thirtieth and Meera must sign the quarter's objectives. Which option do you choose, what do you tell Joshi's 1,400 executives, and what is the first number you put in front of the board in January?

7. A note for the learner

The lens this case asks you to use is the distinction between a vanity metric and an actionable one. A vanity metric is not simply a number that flatters; it is a number whose movement changes no decision. The useful test has two parts. First, can you name what the company would do if the number rose and what it would do if it fell? Second, can a move in the number be traced to a cause somebody controls? Stores onboarded fails both. It is cumulative, so it cannot fall, which means it can never be evidence against anything. And it pools five cohorts, four channels and two market conditions into one figure, so no individual spending decision can be judged against it.

Monthly ordering stores passes both tests. It can fall — and it nearly did during the quarter of heaviest spending, which is precisely the information Kirana Konnect needed and did not have. It decomposes by cohort and channel, so Exhibit 2's sixth column becomes available, and once that column exists the ₹9.5 crore question answers itself differently.

Notice the second mechanism at work, because learners often see only the first. The onboarding definition was written into a field incentive. A metric attached to somebody's pay will be moved through its cheapest mechanism, and the cheapest mechanism here was a single ₹400 order. Nobody behaved dishonestly; the definition simply permitted a cheap path. This is why experienced practitioners ask, before adopting any metric into a compensation plan, how the person being paid would move it without helping the customer.

A well-reasoned answer does not have to abolish the onboarded figure. It has to stop it from allocating money. One defensible path is Option C, executed with more discipline than the option as stated. Meera signs Q3 objectives written exclusively in monthly ordering stores, by cohort, with a named threshold — say, any cohort falling below 40 per cent at ninety days triggers a channel review. She redirects ₹6.5 crore to the distributor and shopkeeper referral channels on the strength of Exhibit 2's sixth column, and honours the field commitments with the remaining ₹3 crore, letting the 5 lakh milestone arrive when it arrives. She adopts Lim's two-week ordering definition from 1 November, giving Joshi five weeks to communicate it. And she puts Exhibit 1 into the Series C data room herself, on the reasoning that a cohort table which the company brings forward and can explain is an asset, while the same table discovered in diligence is a liability.

The judgement to defend is the one about Nair. He is right that investors compare scale, and wrong that this makes the comparison number a steering number. The separation Meera must hold — the same number may communicate and may not allocate — is the whole skill, and the reason Option C is the harder path rather than the softer one.

Dhun: Forty-One Lakh Subscribers

Hyderabad, the night of Sunday 13 September 2026.

1. The night before

Aditi Bhargava had stopped pretending she would sleep. It was a quarter past one on Monday morning, the rain had come back over Hitec City, and her laptop showed two documents side by side. The one on the left was the Series D teaser her chief executive intended to send to four funds on Wednesday. Its second line read: 41 lakh paying subscribers, up 2.4x year on year. The one on the right was a spreadsheet her data scientist in Toronto had sent eleven hours earlier, which showed that 33.1 lakh of those subscribers had arrived through a telecom bundle at ₹6 per user per month, and that fewer than one in nine of them had opened the Dhun app in the preceding thirty days.

Neither document was wrong. That was the part she could not get past.

By Monday evening she owed Sharad Kulkarni, the co-founder and chief executive, a recommendation on three things that had arrived at the same time and that she had until recently regarded as separate problems. The telecom bundle came up for renewal on 30 September; the renewal proposal on the table raised the guaranteed minimum to ₹41 crore a year. The company's largest advertiser, a Dubai wellness brand spending ₹4.6 crore annually, had paused its October flight pending a measurement reconciliation. And Lehar, the AI recommendation feed the product organisation had shipped in March and had been congratulated for all year, was the reason the third-party auditors could no longer match Dhun's impression counts. The board met on Thursday.

2. Company history, and a decision made in 2023

Dhun was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 by Kulkarni and two colleagues from a Telugu television production house, on the observation that a very large number of Indians who would never read a book would listen to one. The app carried audio series in Telugu, Hindi, Tamil, Marathi and Bhojpuri — devotional recitations, romance serials in twelve-minute episodes, true crime, and, from 2022, an examination-preparation library for state civil-service aspirants. It was free with advertising, with a premium tier at ₹99 a month or ₹799 a year. It competed against Kuku FM and Pocket FM for the same listener, against Amazon's Audible and Spotify at the premium end, and against the free devotional content that JioSaavn and YouTube gave away in unlimited quantity.

In August 2023 Dhun made the decision that shaped everything since. It signed a three-year content-bundling agreement with a national telecom operator, under which Dhun Premium was included in two prepaid recharge packs. Dhun received ₹6 per bundled user per month against a guaranteed annual minimum, and the operator received a differentiator in a market where Jio and Airtel had made data itself a commodity. In the first eighteen months the deal delivered 28 lakh bundled subscribers. It also, in the phrase Kulkarni used at the time and had not stopped using, "bought us three years of the right story".

The consequence was structural. Every subsequent plan, board deck and hiring justification had been written in subscriber counts, because subscriber counts were what the deal produced. The growth organisation's objectives, the content commissioning budget by language, and the H2 bonus pool were all indexed to a single line. By FY26 that line stood at 41 lakh, and Dhun's revenue stood at ₹318 crore: ₹96 crore from the bundle, ₹104 crore from direct subscriptions, ₹112 crore from advertising, and ₹6 crore from a small international business Grace Ng ran out of Singapore.

3. The industry

By 2026 the Indian audio market had settled into an awkward shape. Subscription willingness was real but thin: Kuku FM and Pocket FM had demonstrated that Indians would pay for serialised audio fiction at price points between ₹49 and ₹149 a month, while Spotify and Audible had demonstrated that the ceiling above ₹199 was low outside the eight largest cities. Telecom and handset bundling had become the dominant distribution channel for everyone, which meant that the industry's reported subscriber numbers were substantially composed of users who had not chosen the product.

Three external forces pressed on Dhun's numbers directly. First, recurring payments: the Reserve Bank's e-mandate framework and NPCI's UPI Autopay rules meant that a ₹99 monthly subscription required a standing mandate that could fail for a dozen reasons, and Google Play's billing share took a further cut on Android, where 94 per cent of Dhun's direct subscribers transacted. Second, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act: Dhun's consent-notice rollout in July 2026 had been well executed legally and clumsily executed technically, and a share of listeners now declined the analytics consent that had previously been implicit. Third, advertising measurement: brands buying audio inventory in India had begun demanding third-party verification of completed listens rather than accepting publisher-reported impressions, a shift the Dubai account had led.

Dhun's exposure to global markets was modest in revenue and large in attention. Ng's Singapore operation had replicated the bundle model with two Southeast Asian operators, at economics nobody had examined closely. Rajiv Menon sold advertising from New Jersey to diaspora-facing and Gulf brands, of which the Dubai wellness brand was the largest by a distance.

4. The situation in detail

In January 2026 Dhun's listening minutes per daily active user had been 26.4. The product organisation's single most important objective for FY27, agreed in February, was to raise it to 34. Karthik Subramanian, the data scientist in Toronto who had joined from a video recommendation team, proposed that the fastest route was to replace the app's editorially curated home screen with a ranked feed. Lehar shipped to 100 per cent of users on 18 March 2026, and by August minutes per daily active user stood at 33.8.

What was believed in March: that minutes per active user was the company's best available proxy for whether listeners valued the product, and that raising it would raise both subscription conversion and advertising inventory. Both propositions had been argued rather than tested; the model's objective function rewarded predicted session length, and no holdout group had been maintained past the first two weeks because holding back the feed was judged to cost inventory.

What has since turned out to be more complicated. On 12 April, Pranav Deshpande in Pune changed the session-timeout parameter in the analytics pipeline from thirty minutes to a hundred and twenty, to stop devotional listeners who paused between recitations from being split into multiple sessions. The change was reasonable on its own terms. It was applied forward only, without backfill, and it mechanically lengthened measured sessions for every user whose listening had gaps — which, for an app played in kitchens and on scooters, is most of them. Deshpande noted the change in a pull-request description. Nobody read it.

On 2 July the DPDP consent notice went live. Analytics consent was declined by roughly 14 per cent of returning users, and events from those users stopped arriving. The effect on rates was not neutral: the decliners skewed towards older Android devices in smaller cities, which is also where the devotional and examination content over-indexed.

On 21 August, Menon forwarded a reconciliation from the Dubai advertiser's measurement partner. Dhun had billed for 61.2 crore completed listens in the quarter; the partner had verified 38.9 crore. The largest single category of difference was inventory served into sessions where the app was in the background with no user interaction for more than forty minutes — sessions Lehar's autoplay chaining had made common, and which the new timeout parameter had made invisible as a discontinuity.

On 4 September, Subramanian ran the retention pull that Bhargava had asked for in July and had twice been deprioritised. Week-eight retention for direct paying subscribers acquired after the Lehar launch was 4.6 percentage points below the pre-launch cohorts. 7. The options as Bhargava currently sees them

Sitting in front of her, written out at half past midnight on a single page, were four courses of action. She had written them as product decisions, which is how she had been trained to write them.

Turn off autoplay chaining. Lehar keeps ranking but stops continuing into unattended sessions. The measurement gap in Exhibit 3 narrows on its own, the Dubai account probably returns, and minutes per active user falls — by an amount nobody can forecast, because the definitional change is tangled with the behavioural one. The FY27 objective of 34.0 becomes unreachable, which means the product organisation misses the only objective the board has seen it commit to.

Renew the bundle on the proposed terms and hold the headline. The Series D proceeds on 41 lakh, Malhotra reaches 45, Ng keeps her reference deal, and Exhibit 6's downside case — a contribution of negative ₹35 crore if bundled volume falls — is accepted as the price of the story. Bhargava's own estimate is that the odds of the downside case are materially better than the operator's projections imply, because the operator now controls the volume and no longer has a per-user incentive to grow it.

Do not renew, and restate. Dhun reports 7.3 lakh direct paying subscribers plus a bundled reach figure, reprices advertising on the verified definition, and enters the Series D as a smaller company with cleaner numbers. Revenue falls by roughly ₹96 crore against a cost base that does not fall as fast, and the round is a different round. Kulkarni has not agreed to consider this and Bhargava has not yet asked him directly.

Fix the measurement first and decide in November. Commission the backfill, restate Exhibit 2 on a single definition, stand up a holdout for Lehar, and reconcile Exhibit 3 with finance. Six weeks of two engineers, one analyst, and a bundle renewal deadline of 30 September that will not move.

What she had not written on the page, and had begun to suspect at around one o'clock, was that all four options took as given the thing most in question: that the company's problem was which product change to make, rather than which number the company would allow to govern it. Every one of her four options was reversible within a year. The decision about what Dhun would be measured by — in its objectives, its bonus pool, its royalty allocation, its advertiser contracts and its Series D — was not.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The bundle renewal must be signed or declined by 30 September; the operator's procurement cycle closes and the existing agreement lapses with no extension clause. The board meets on Thursday 17 September and expects a recommendation on the renewal and a position on the advertising reconciliation. The Series D teaser is scheduled to go out on Wednesday 16 September, before the board meets, which Bhargava had noticed only that evening.

Money: Dhun holds ₹212 crore of cash against an FY27 operating plan that assumes ₹41 crore of bundle revenue and ₹138 crore of advertising. Removing the bundle without repricing the plan implies roughly fourteen months of runway. Menon's unauthorised ₹40 lakh make-good is not in the plan. People: the backfill requires Deshpande and one other engineer for six weeks, which means the Diwali content-release tooling slips; Hoffmann may not be there in October; Malhotra's team of sixty has a bonus pool that is already communicated. Regulation: the DPDP consent framework cannot be loosened to recover the missing events, and the RBI e-mandate flow cannot be shortened. Contracts: the FMCG and auto insertion orders do not specify an impression definition, which means a restatement is a commercial negotiation rather than a correction, across nine advertisers and one exchange.

10. Half past two

The rain had eased. Bhargava had written one more line at the bottom of the page and had not decided whether it was an insight or an excuse: the number is not wrong, it is just not ours to steer by any more. She read Kulkarni's email again and found that she could not, at two in the morning, produce the list of three decisions he had asked for — not because the list did not exist, but because every item she thought of turned out to belong to somebody else.

Subramanian would be awake in Toronto in four hours. Ng wanted her two weeks' notice. Al Suwaidi wanted one definition, stated and held. Deshpande wanted somebody to say the April change had been reasonable. Malhotra wanted the renewal, and was not wrong that nothing else reached 45 lakh. Somewhere in the four options on the page was the one she would recommend on Thursday, and she closed the laptop without knowing which.
